rows.section: Observable by a package: owned local editor commands
rows.gnu: GNU supplies the complete command/completion, Dired and file policy libraries.
rows.romacs: The default workspace uses separate Romacs-owned Lisp orchestration: interactive command-name completion/history and a read-only local directory browser with GNU-style long metadata columns, semantic filename faces and n/p/RET/^/g/q. The C-locale ordinary-file listing matches the GNU reference; locale collation, ACL/security indicators and special-device size columns are not implemented. Control-character filenames remain explicitly escaped on one row. Local UTF-8 files and directories share native visits; remote handlers, listing switches, Dired mutation commands and the full GNU coding/mode lifecycle remain unsupported (file coding: VM2-WORKSPACE-CODING). The pristine GNU Lisp tree is unchanged; GNU-only startup does not install these owned modules.
rows.why: A useful slim editor path independent of GNU's full diagnostic/startup dependencies. Maintained GUI command tests and private native-keyboard journeys cover the supported slice, not full GNU API parity.

rows.section: Observable by a package: owned local editor commands
rows.mechanism: `erase-buffer` rejection in a narrowed read-only buffer
rows.gnu: The pinned GNU implementation widens before reporting `buffer-read-only`, changing the accessible region despite rejection.
rows.romacs: The native buffer-level guard runs before widening, preserving text, point, restriction and modification ticks on rejection. Any non-nil `inhibit-read-only` bypasses the buffer-level guard; text-property protection is a separate boundary.
rows.why: Deliberate failure-state preservation for editor-owned read-only views. Live pinned GNU probes distinguish the widening side effect; maintained text/byte-buffer tests assert the safer contract and typed condition/data identity.

rows.section: Observable by a package: scoped GUI command bootstrap
rows.gnu: GNU's dumped image normally supplies all of simple.el.
rows.romacs: When simple.el stops at an unrelated unsupported declaration, the GUI separately evaluates the exact source forms for the line-motion command dependency group. Existing definitions are never replaced; the original partial-file result and each supplemental source line remain reported.
rows.why: Decouples C-a/C-e from generic-function bootstrap without native command stand-ins or edits to GNU Lisp; scoped source-loading and original command-loop tests cover it.

rows.section: Observable by a package: columns and minibuffer identity
rows.gnu: GNU accounts for display tables, invisibility and composition, and `current-column` caches its last answer by point and modification count (so a `tab-width` change alone can leave it stale).
rows.romacs: Native Unicode text width, tab stops and caret controls are counted without moving point; display-property overrides are not projected, and non-UTF-8 byte text refuses.
rows.why: Plain-text command-motion slice, not a complete display-table implementation.

rows.section: Observable by a package: columns and minibuffer identity
rows.gnu: GNU retains every initialized minibuffer and recognizes active enclosing recursive levels.
rows.romacs: The predicate recognizes native minibuffer-window buffer identities and current activation. Hidden buffers from enclosing recursive levels are not tracked by this predicate.
rows.why: Uses the current native window model rather than buffer-name heuristics.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.mechanism: Save-side path expansion, coding and handlers
rows.gnu: GNU dispatches expansion/directory helpers and supports filename coding.
rows.romacs: Expansion and its helpers (`directory-file-name`, `file-name-nondirectory` in expand_cp_target) dispatch their handlers in GNU's order, through Lisp where one is selected, then the operation's own handler runs. Non-UTF-8 filename coding and nonrepresentable byte paths remain refused.
rows.why: The full filename codec is not implemented. `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/filesave/README.md`, `evidence/handler-local/`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU may prompt on integer overwrite arguments and implements cross-device copying.
rows.romacs: Collision with integer confirmation and EXDEV explicitly refuse without performing copy/delete. Linux atomic no-replace syscall failures propagate; no racy fallback.
rows.why: Local atomic rename subset. `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/filesave/gnu.json`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: An integer OK-IF-ALREADY-EXISTS that meets an existing name asks `yes-or-no-p` (batch reads stdin). PRESERVE-PERMISSIONS copies extended (POSIX or NFSv4) ACLs; an SELinux context only in a libselinux build, which the pin is not. `file-name-all-completions` decodes entries with `file-name-coding-system`.
rows.romacs: An integer proceeds while the name is free and refuses with `VM2 <operation> interactive overwrite confirmation` on a collision, before writing. PRESERVE-PERMISSIONS refuses before creating NEWNAME when the source carries an extended ACL. Listing refuses non-UTF-8 file-name coding and a non-UTF-8 entry that passes the prefix test, and gives `./` and `../` first, then `read_dir` order (both readdir). Handlers dispatch as GNU's; expansion handlers refuse (VM2-SAVE-PATH).
rows.why: No prompt from a leaf; the Hermes and gnosis callers pass nil or t. Oracle test `file_names_links_and_copies_match_gnu` (`crates/romacs-vm/tests/real_ert_load.rs`) compares values, errors and the resulting files with pinned GNU.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU appends six randomized alphanumeric characters without creating a file.
rows.romacs: Same shape/noncreation; random sequence is not GNU PRNG sequence equality.
rows.why: Names are not reservations. `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/filesave/README.md`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU uses symlink interlocks, local PID/boot checks and automatic edit/save lifecycle locking.
rows.romacs: `lock-file` and `unlock-file` dispatch their handlers and implement symlink interlocks, stale removal and conflict callbacks; a buffer's first modification locks its truename (`rlisp/vm/insdel.el`), `restore-buffer-modified-p` and `set-buffer-modified-p` lock or unlock it as the state flips, `kill-buffer` unlocks a modified buffer's file, `kill-emacs` unlocks every modified buffer's (unlock_all_files), `write-region` locks LOCKNAME before writing and unlocks it after (but for an auto-save), and a visit unlocks the truename and the name, as GNU does. Where GNU's C calls `Flock_file` or `Funlock_file` directly, Romacs calls `lock-file` or `unlock-file` as Lisp functions, so advice on them applies. Before files.el defines `make-lock-file-name` (the bare regime) a file has no lock name. Some nested callback errors propagate instead of redirecting to unlock error handling. Nonregular lock files refuse, link-less filesystem fallback and cross-host boot databases are absent. The boot field is omitted (GNU-supported legacy identity) because `/proc/stat` differs from GNU gnulib boot time on this host; live local PID locks are conservatively retained regardless of the supplied boot field. Reboot/PID-reuse stale detection is therefore unimplemented and may report a false conflict instead of deleting a live owner. Current login environment supplies identity; subsequent changes may affect it.
rows.why: Explicit native locking slice, not full lifecycle parity. `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/filelock-save/REPORT.md`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: Pinned GNU is built with libacl and without libselinux: `file-acl` is `acl_to_text` of `acl_get_file`'s access ACL (named entries by name, `\t#effective:` where a mask withholds rights), nil for a missing file or an error `acl_errno_valid` rejects; `set-file-acl` is `acl_from_text` then `acl_set_file`, t on success, nil for invalid text or a non-string; a context is `(nil nil nil nil)` and setting one returns nil, each after its handler.
rows.romacs: Read and written as the `system.posix_acl_access` attribute (the mode bits when it is absent), transcribing libacl's text forms; contexts as pinned GNU. `acl_from_text` is transcribed for access entries (long and one-letter tags, names or numbers, comma or newline separators, `#` comments); `default:` entries are refused as invalid text, so nil.
rows.why: `tests/real_ert_load.rs` `fileio_defuns_match_gnu`, against pinned GNU with an ACL made by `setfacl`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: `fileio.c:6315` runs `auto-save-hook` safely, writes `auto-save-list-file-name` with stdio, auto-saves each modified buffer (those without a `write-region` handler first) with `auto_saving` set (the visited file's mode, `utf-8-emacs` unless into the visited file, no lock, no fsync), reports an error through `display-warning`, disables a buffer that shrank a lot, and is also run by the command loop after `auto-save-interval` events or `auto-save-timeout` idle seconds (`record_auto_save` resets that count).
rows.romacs: The subr's loop is a Lisp transcription (`rlisp/vm/auto-save.el`) over native `romacs--auto-save-1` (auto_save_1), `romacs--auto-save-done`, `romacs--auto-save-failure-time` and `romacs--write-auto-save-list`; `write-region` honours the auto-saving state as GNU's does. The message stack is kept as the current message. Where GNU's C calls `write-region`, `file-modes` or `restore-buffer-modified-p` directly, Romacs calls them as Lisp functions, so advice on them applies.
rows.why: `tests/real_ert_load.rs` `fileio_defuns_match_gnu` compares an auto-save, its list file and modes with pinned GNU.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: `fileio.c:2647` answers from the platform: nil on GNU/Linux, where no `_PC_CASE_*` pathconf exists, without asking the filesystem; t on MS-Windows and Cygwin; macOS asks `pathconf (_PC_CASE_SENSITIVE)`, walking up while it cannot tell. Handlers run first.
rows.romacs: Handlers run first. On Linux Romacs measures where GNU assumes nil: from the name's directory (the name itself when it is a directory, else the directory it is in, walking up to the nearest that exists), one `statfs` reads the filesystem type. vfat and msdos (`MSDOS_SUPER_MAGIC` 0x4d44), exFAT (0x2011bab0), the old ntfs driver (0x5346544e, case-insensitive unless mounted `case_sensitive=yes`), HFS (0x4244) and HFS+ (0x482b) answer t; an HFSX volume, which may be case-sensitive, answers t as well. On ext2/3/4 (0xef53), f2fs (0xf2f52010) and tmpfs (0x01021994), one `FS_IOC_GETFLAGS` on the directory, opened `O_DIRECTORY` and `O_NOFOLLOW`, answers t when `FS_CASEFOLD_FL` is set. Every other filesystem answers nil, among them ntfs3 (case-sensitive unless mounted `nocase`, which statfs cannot show), CIFS and SMB2 (the server and mount options decide) and FUSE. Any error answers nil, as GNU does when it cannot tell; nothing signals for an unknown answer, and no directory is listed, so a directory's size never matters. A world build records the walk's entry types (not their times), the filesystem type and the flags as keyed probes, and restore asks them again; its confined thread reads flags through an unconfined thread that makes only that query. A unibyte non-ASCII name (ENCODE_FILE's output, which `set-auto-coding` passes on) names the file its UTF-8 bytes spell; other bytes are refused. Off Linux: t on MS-Windows, else nil (no macOS pathconf).
rows.why: Owner explicitly requires actual measurement rather than a platform constant; this keeps it. The earlier directory-entry measurement signalled for a directory over 4096 entries and broke startup from a large working, home or temporary directory. Qualified for real only on a casefold tmpfs made in a private user and mount namespace (`filename_case_measures_a_real_casefold_directory`, `crates/romacs-vm/tests/savejourney.rs`); no real vfat, exFAT, NTFS, HFS, ext4 or f2fs casefold mount has been qualified, and those answers rest on the magic numbers and the classifier's unit tests (`savejourney.rs` `case_tests`). Beside a case-sensitive filesystem, and a directory of 4100 entries, answers match pinned GNU (`filename_case_matches_gnu_beside_a_huge_directory`).

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU performs full codec conversion.
rows.romacs: `encode-coding-string` and `decode-coding-string` support nil/no-conversion, UTF-8 and raw-text coding systems, aliases, EOL conversion, simple BOM handling, NOCOPY and last-coding-system-used. GNU ASCII fast paths are retained. Other conversion codecs, coding hooks, BOM-pair detection and buffer destinations explicitly refuse.
rows.why: This is a bounded string-conversion domain, checked against pinned GNU in `tests/coding_strings.rs`; it does not establish general codec or file-coding parity.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU supports full filename/ID coding and attribute platform semantics.
rows.romacs: Numeric and named-ID file-attributes and local symlink reads are implemented; unresolved user/group lookups fall back to numeric IDs. Non-UTF-8 symlink targets refuse; stat error and concurrent-change domains are not fully qualified.
rows.why: Scoped native blockers; details in `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/savejourney/native-followup.md`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: save batch (WIP, not accepted)
rows.gnu: GNU formats the complete event/sequence and string-property domain.
rows.romacs: Character/string/vector/list formatting, prefix/ESC folding and symbolic event formatting implemented. Compound events explicitly refuse; rich properties and mixed unibyte formatting remain partial.
rows.why: Needed by real GNU help.el prerequisite, not claimed full parity. `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/savejourney/continue-report.md`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: executable image immutability
rows.mechanism: Object-granularity executable-image rehydration cost; opt-in raw-image freeze
rows.gnu: GNU's writable dumped world permits mutation without copying these roots. Live pinned GNU preserves mixed code/data/plist identity, and byte-compiled literals remain mutable.
rows.romacs: Executable restoration copies every reachable supported Lisp object (cons/string), including code literals, plists, condition properties and captures, with one identity memo. Cold IR remains mapped and undecoded: generated uninterned symbol slots root the private literal objects for later decoding and moving GC. The yank-menu fixture costs exactly **4 private Lisp objects / 195 bytes**; this excludes native metadata allocations. Bare `Vm::new` and raw data-image attachment remain **0 / 0** independently. The mixed fixture preserves `eq` and makes mutation through the variable visible to its function, while another strand remains unchanged. Executable Lisp objects are not frozen. Explicit raw `ImageBuilder` graphs remain immutable and their mutation is refused.
rows.why: The retained raw-image freeze is an explicit embedding boundary, not GNU's writable dump semantics. Per-strand heaps share immutable encoded bytes, never mutable Lisp objects or page-level copy-on-write. Copy-on-write semantics are realized eagerly at executable restoration, at the measured **4 objects / 195 bytes** fixture cost rather than GNU's zero-copy writable-dump access. Eager object rehydration and existing symbol roots preserve cross-root and cold-code aliasing without a new GC root class or image-page writes. This is an allocation-cost divergence, not a mutation/identity divergence. Tests: `tests/code_image.rs`, `code_image::image_alias_tests`; oracle: `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/image-freeze-oracle.json`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.gnu: Not in GNU. GNU's concurrency is `make-thread` (cooperative, one global lock); an uncaught error in a thread is stored in `thread-last-error` and `thread-join` returns normally.
rows.romacs: Worker VMs are child processes that adopt the spawner's world (`--isolate`), run `(apply FUNCTION ARGS)` on frozen arguments and answer with a frozen result or the error, delivered at wait points (the command loop's idle, `isolate-await`). `isolate-await` re-signals the worker's error with its condition and transportable data, defining an unknown condition with the worker's `error-conditions` ancestry; unfreezable data elements arrive as `(isolate-unfreezable PRINTED)`. A worker's death resolves its futures with `isolate-died`, a kill with `isolate-killed`. The worker's backtrace is not transported (`isolate-error-backtrace` stays nil). `isolate-interrupt` quits CPU-bound Lisp at the engine's safepoints, honouring `inhibit-quit`; a job blocked in a primitive (a `call-process` wait) is not interrupted until it returns, and `isolate-kill` follows after `isolate-interrupt-timeout`. GNU's `make-thread` family is not implemented (void).
rows.why: A package observes these only by calling them. Re-signalling is deliberate: a background job's failure must reach the code that asked for it. Tests: `crates/romacs-vm/tests/isolates.rs`, `tests/isolate_interrupt.rs`; design: vm-concurrency note §4.

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.mechanism: Writes to frozen and executable-image objects
rows.gnu: GNU raises `(error "Attempt to modify read-only object" OBJ)` for pure-space and constant strings (`CHECK_IMPURE`); it has no user-creatable read-only conses, vectors, records, bool-vectors, char-tables or hash tables.
rows.romacs: `freeze` copies a value graph (conses, strings with their text properties, vectors, records, floats, bignums, bool-vectors, char-tables, non-weak hash tables, symbols by name) into an immutable region; every mutator of such an object (`setcar`, `setcdr`, `nreverse`, `nconc`, `sort`, `delq` past the head, `aset`, `fillarray`, `clear-string`, the text-property writers, `puthash`, `remhash`, `clrhash`, `set-char-table-range`, `set-char-table-parent`, `set-char-table-extra-slot`, `modify-category-entry`) signals GNU's read-only error with the object, as do writes to executable-image strings and conses (which signalled a VM2 text before). `copy-sequence` and `thaw` give private copies. Markers, overlays, buffers, processes, windows, frames, closures, subrs, weak tables, obarrays, finalizers, sqlite handles and syntax tables refuse to freeze with `(error "Cannot freeze" OBJ PATH)`.
rows.why: One refusal for every frozen write, GNU's own error. Tests: `crates/romacs-vm/src/frozen_tests.rs` (`every_mutator_refuses_with_gnus_read_only_error`).

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.gnu: GNU has no boundary: any function object is callable anywhere.
rows.romacs: `isolate-spawn` accepts a symbol (the worker calls its own definition, autoloading as needed) or a lambda form, a list the worker evaluates, with free variables supplied by `:bindings`; a closure object signals `(error "Cannot send closure" FN)`.
rows.why: Closure export (literal identity, symbol relocation, macro and compiler dependencies, captures) is unresolved; design note §3.3, M6.

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.mechanism: What a worker sees of the spawner
rows.gnu: n/a (one heap).
rows.romacs: A worker starts from the world's globals plus `isolate-inherited-variables` (thawed into worker-owned copies) and a job's `:bindings`; it never sees the spawner's later `setq`s, loaded packages or user init. A pooled worker keeps its own symbol values between jobs of the same `:require` set; a job that changed `features` retires its worker from the pool.
rows.why: Racket's and Python's contract for isolated interpreters; design §3.5, §7.

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.mechanism: Frame and window queries in a worker
rows.gnu: n/a.
rows.romacs: A worker has the batch session's initial frame and terminal: `display-graphic-p` is nil, `frame-width` and friends answer as in `emacs --batch`.
rows.why: A worker owns no display.

rows.section: Observable by a package: isolates and frozen values
rows.gnu: Enumerate (`project-files`) and search (`xref-matches-in-files`) synchronously; the session blocks until the prompt or the xref buffer appears.
rows.romacs: When a worker of the session's own world stands prepared and idle, the enumeration and the grep run in it; the command returns to the command loop at once and continues, with the identical candidate list or xref matches, when the result arrives: the prompt or xref buffer appears then, and keys typed meanwhile run their commands. Without such a worker the GNU definitions run unchanged and a worker is warmed for the next command once the session idles; `project-find-regexp` warms its worker while the regexp is typed, so its first run normally finds it ready; a worker that will not take the job after all (queue full, process gone) is passed over the same way. The commands never wait for a worker's boot. Without a world (a source boot, batch) nothing is warmed.
rows.why: The candidate list and the matches are the worker's `project-files` and `xref-matches-in-files` over the same project; only the timing of the prompt differs. Live journey: `crates/romacs-vm-gui/harness/isolates_live.py`.

rows.gnu: GNU `font.c:2144-2166` scores candidate size including fixed-size fonts, DPI and average-width mismatch, with factor-of-two rejection; `xfaces.c:5850-5907` validates, stores and invalidates realized faces.
rows.romacs: Exact validation accepts duplicates and returns nil, without changing `face-font-selection-order`. Order is stored in VM display state, published to layout, consumed by resolver ranking, and changed orders invalidate previous face publications and resolver primary/character caches. The `:height` versus other-attribute trade-off is **NOT REPRODUCED**: order is honoured only to the extent current StyleScore expresses it (width/weight/slant; Height has zero distance).
rows.why: Fontconfig catalog discards non-scalable candidates and retains no size/DPI fields (`romacs-font/src/fontconfig_catalog.rs:279`); VM2 snapshot drops width/weight/slant (`romacs-vm/src/display.rs:631-636` in lane base); layout Face cannot carry them (`romacs-layout-input/src/lib.rs:23-28` in lane base); StyleScore has fixed default priority and no size term (`romacs-font/src/style.rs:148-179` in lane base). Observable font selection can therefore differ. Widening this coordinated DISPLAY substrate is deferred by owner decision, not impossible. Live pinned validation witnesses: `crates/romacs-vm/tools/primh/font-selection-specs/internal-set-font-selection-order.json`; cache/ranking assertions: `romacs-font/src/resolver/tests/selection_order_test.rs`. Configured family alternatives are now copied/interned into a traced VM root, published as owned state, and successful setters always invalidate previous face publications and resolver primary/character answers. The scalable resolver still uses its existing FontsetPolicy: consuming the new GNU alternative rows is deferred, not approximated with Rust lowercase (GNU uses case-table uppercase comparison, including final-sigma equivalence and Lisp symbol identity).

rows.mechanism: Alternative-font setters and inherited intern/casing substrate
rows.gnu: GNU family setter copies both list-spine levels, interns strings in the current obarray, stores/returns the converted alist and unconditionally frees realized faces. Registry setter instead calls full current-buffer `downcase`.
rows.romacs: Family setter implements shape/error/copy/storage/invalidation semantics; inherited initial-obarray interning loses symbol-name properties and rejects non-UTF8 names. Registry setter remains absent, rather than introducing default-only lowercase.
rows.why: Live family corpus `font-alternative-specs/internal-set-alternative-font-family-alist.json`: `/0045` and `/0046` VALUE pins (symbol-name properties); `/0047` SIGNAL-VS-VALUE pin (unibyte name). Excluded decimal-bignum probe fails in existing reader before invocation (VM2-READ4); excluded custom-case-table probe requires absent current-case-table/set-case-table substrate. Registry requires GNU casetab.c validation/derived-table regeneration and four buffer case-table roots, plus casefiddle.c special lowercase/string semantics; bounded port stopped before a partial implementation.

rows.mechanism: `sort` default comparison, list identity and callback effects
rows.gnu: Default comparator is native `value<`; stable timsort writes sorted elements back into the original list cons cells and exposes its callback/mutation order.
rows.romacs: Default `value<` compares the runtime's numbers, strings, symbols, lists, vectors, bool-vectors, records, markers and buffers with GNU ordering, mismatch data and depth limits; process and symbol-with-position objects remain unavailable. Explicit comparators and keyword parsing work, with stable small-input natural-run/binary insertion. Inputs of 64 or more use stable insertion sort, with differing callback count/order and complexity; intermediate vector mutation/error effects are not matched.
rows.why: Partial implementation, not complete GNU sort parity. Maintained value-order tests cover default sorts, mixed numeric precision, raw-byte names, circular lists and depth-limit recovery. Live corpus `tools/primh/evidence/sort.json` and the small-sort probes retain the separate sort limitations.

rows.mechanism: `mapconcat` property preservation and absent bool-vector constructor
rows.gnu: Concatenation preserves properties from mapped strings and separators; bool-vectors are valid sequences.
rows.romacs: Inherited native concat drops properties (`mapconcat/0021`, GNU bold versus nil). Bool-vector witness stops at missing make-bool-vector (`/0016`).
rows.why: Shared concatenation/property and representation boundaries; live corpus and exact witnesses in `evidence/leaf-sequences/divergences.json`. Pinned GNU itself aborts when a mapping callback truncates its active list; excluded crashing witness retained in pin-probes.json, not synthesized as a condition.

rows.mechanism: The debugger on the signal path, and the command loop's error report
rows.gnu: eval.c `signal_or_quit` considers the debugger for an error with `debug-on-signal`, when no handler catches it, or when the catching clause lists `debug` or is C's `error` (the command loop's and top level's); `maybe_call_debugger` then asks `inhibit-debugger`, `debug-on-error` (or `debug-on-quit`), `debug-ignored-errors` and once per input event, and `call_debugger` applies `debugger` to `(error ERROR)`. keyboard.c `cmd_error` passes the error, its macro context and `Vsignaling_function` (the frame below the top one at the signal, past `error`) to `command-error-function`, whose default rings the bell and prints the message to the echo area, *Messages* logging the caller before it
rows.romacs: The same rule in `threaded_signal.rs` `debugger_wanted` for every signal, those primitives raise included, with the rest in `romacs--call-debugger-p` (rlisp/vm/prelude.el) and the call in the signal path's own form, so the debugger's frame sits on the signalling one; the command loop's and batch top level's catch-all is `(debug t)` (rlisp/vm/keyboard.el, `crates/romacs-vm-gui/src/batch.rs`), and its report is `command-error-function` with the caller a `handler-bind` reads from the frames (`romacs--note-signaling-function`). Different: (1) a quit is never continued: a debugger returning from one lets it unwind, where GNU resumes code that `maybe_quit` stopped (C-g is no asynchronous quit, VM2-HOSTIN1); (2) batch top level prints no backtrace for each error (top_level_2's `debug-early--handler`, VM2-ERRTEXT1); (3) the caller *Messages* names comes from Romacs's frames, which record every primitive call: where pinned GNU's byte code inlines a primitive (`insert`, `forward-char`, `goto-char` in compiled code) or its native code calls one, GNU names the caller one level further out; a `signal` frame under `error` or `user-error` is skipped, as pinned GNU's native-compiled subr.el records none
rows.why: **Visible to the user** in *Messages* for (3). `crates/romacs-vm/tests/debugger_entry.rs` (32 cases against pinned GNU batch); `crates/romacs-vm-gui/harness/command_errors_live.py` against pinned GNU pgtk: command errors' echo, *Messages* and bells, M-: (car 1) and a `debug-on-error` command entering *Backtrace*, q and c

rows.gnu: `(symbol-value 2)` signals `(wrong-type-argument symbolp 2)`.
rows.romacs: Signals `(wrong-type-argument listp 2)`.
rows.why: Existing variable-access condition-data gap exposed by internal-make-var-non-special/0018; retained VALUE class pin, no invented oracle answer.

rows.gnu: `Felt` (fns.c:1853) accepts bool-vectors and rejects records/byte-code objects with `wrong-type-argument sequencep`; `Faref` accepting the latter does not make them arrays for Felt.
rows.romacs: Lists, strings, vectors, bool-vectors and existing char-tables work. The two bool-vector missing pins were removed after live GNU replay. Remaining record/byte-compile construction witnesses retain their existing limitations. These are not fake vectors or successful nil results, and the construction errors are NOT claimed to equal GNU's elt errors.
rows.why: Remaining construction boundaries are recorded in `tools/primh/evidence/elt.json`. Closure rejection itself agrees with GNU when only condition and predicate are inspected.

rows.gnu: Printer serializes the circular input `(1 2 1 2 . #2)` in the corpus control.
rows.romacs: Refuses circular list printing without `print-circle`; actual elt circular access is tested successfully at maximum fixnum.
rows.why: Existing printer gap, 1 PRINTER witness in `tools/primh/evidence/elt.json`; not an elt semantic alternative.

rows.mechanism: `elt` on the separate native syntax-table kind
rows.gnu: `(elt (standard-syntax-table) 97)` returns a syntax descriptor cons, because GNU syntax tables are char-tables.
rows.romacs: Refuses with `(wrong-type-argument sequencep TABLE)` rather than inventing a descriptor. This is NOT GNU-equivalent for that valid input. Ordinary CharTable objects are supported, but VM2's separate regexp-host SyntaxTable is not.

rows.gnu: GNU counts its own typed allocation pools and vectorlike objects.
rows.romacs: Counts describe Romacs storage: cons arena entries/reserve; symbol slots excluding private binding slots and freed slots; string headers and actual string bytes; ordinary vector arena entries and element slots/reserve; float arena entries; both buffer variants. Mixed object-arena reserve is not attributed to strings or floats (their typed free pools are empty). SIZE is the corresponding fixed Romacs storage, excluding variable backing allocations; buffers use the shared object-arena slot size. Non-vector Rust objects are not claimed as GNU pseudovectors.

rows.gnu: `consing_threshold` (`alloc.c:5740-5809`) collects once the bytes allocated since the last GC exceed max(`gc-cons-threshold`, 80000) or, for a float `gc-cons-percentage` (default 0.1), that fraction of the live heap's bytes plus half the bytes allocated since; a percentage of 2 or more never collects.
rows.romacs: The same rule, read live from both variables, with GNU's defaults (800000, 0.1), in Romacs units: allocation counts heap objects at 16 bytes each (a GNU cons), and the live heap is what a collection traverses, the objects the last collection retained plus the compiled code units (IR ops and lowered instructions) it traced. The percentage is scaled by 17 (`PERCENTAGE_SCALE`), so GNU's 0.1 collects after about 11.3 traced heaps, and the scaled value is clamped to 1.8 (`MAX_SCALED_PERCENTAGE`): any setting from about 0.106 up, gcmh-style 0.2 to 1.0 included, defers to 18 traced heaps, and none reaches GNU's never-collect point. Negative and NaN settings leave the threshold alone. An embedder's `Vm::set_collection_floor` replaces both variables (as GNU's memory-full state replaces them) with the floor rule tests and `--gc-floor` use.
rows.why: A Romacs collection moves objects and walks compiled code, so it costs more per traced unit than GNU's: unscaled, 0.1 did 65 collections on the census file, +30% instructions over the uninhibited base. Scaled, a config written for GNU gets proportional behaviour: restoring 0.1 after startup is the default, and raising either variable defers collection. The scale is the smallest measured that is not slower than the 60ebf00b base, which never collects inside a load. Frame-pointer gate builds on the owner's machine, each loading its own worktree's Lisp, on a long nested load (15M allocating iterations in a `require`d file); for each scale: instructions against the base's 121.00G, collections and peak RSS (base 2.09 GB): 15, +0.8%, 14, 0.76 GB; 16, +0.2%, 10, 0.79 GB; 17, −0.5%, 8, 0.85 GB; 18 (and 20, 30 or 45, which the 1.8 clamp makes the same), −0.5%, 7, 1.16 GB; 20 with a 3.0 clamp (a scaled 2 or more never collects proportionally), −0.3%, 3–4, 2.22 GB. Over 12 rotating triples of the base, 15 and 17 (load 2.9–4.0), the means of wall, user and sys time, instructions, collections and peak RSS: base 11.26, 9.95 and 1.20 s, 121.00G, 0, 2.10 GB; 15 11.17, 10.23 and 0.85 s, 121.97G, 14, 0.78 GB; 17 10.83, 9.73 and 1.02 s, 120.37G, 8, 0.85 GB. Paired against the base, 15 is −0.10 s in wall time (standard error 0.10 s) and 17 is −0.43 s (0.11 s), faster in 10 of 12 pairs. At 17 against the base, the `--loadup` bootstrap: −1.7% instructions (64.45G vs 65.57G, 30 collections, as at 15), peak RSS 236–241 MB vs 273–278 MB. The census file: −1.3% (59.29G vs 60.10G, 5 collections), 796–806 MB vs 801–812 MB. GUI per key (`perkey_live`, `--loadup`, 200 lines): self-insert 87.8M vs 90.5M instructions, C-n 297.6M vs 297.0M, C-f 126.4M vs 129.2M. In the long load's collections, sweep and compaction take about 55% of the time, marking about 29% and the compiled-code walk about 9%. Tests: `crates/romacs-vm/tests/garbage_collect.rs`, `gc::tests`.

rows.gnu: `alloc.c:6044` returns nil without collecting when collection is inhibited; otherwise GNU may collect inside any Lisp call, its conservative stack scan keeping C locals alive.
rows.romacs: Collection runs only where no native frame keeps heap Values in untraced Rust storage (`Vm::may_collect`): every running engine other than the collecting one is suspended (state, code and registers traced), no compiler builder is open, and no watcher notification comes from a native writer that has not rooted its frame. Native frames keep later-used Values in traced storage (a root frame, a binding, a `#:` slot); `crates/romacs-vm/tests/fixtures/reentry-sites.txt` classifies every reentry call site. So `eval`, `load`, `require`, `macroexpand`, autoloads, lazy bodies, `signal-hook-function`, handler-bind callbacks, reader callbacks, `(lambda ...)` list calls and watchers of `setq`, `let` and its unwinding in compiled code collect. Inhibited, and `garbage-collect` returns nil: Lisp a leaf, T2 continuation or legacy primitive reaches without suspending its engine (watchers of `set`, `set-default`, `defvaralias`, `makunbound` and other writes made inside primitives, a `defalias-fset-function`, a face's function `:height`); watchers of variables the loader and other native code bind or set; and macro expansion while a compiler builder is open.
rows.why: A Rust frame cannot be scanned conservatively: each inhibited region holds Values in locals that have not been audited for a moving collection. The heap grows only within one such call, never across a load, prompt or `eval`. No collection or fake statistics are claimed in those regions. Tests: `crates/romacs-vm/tests/gc_reentry.rs` (forced moving collections, `ROMACS_GC_STRESS`), `tests/reentry_sites.rs`.

rows.gnu: `make-finalizer` (`alloc.c:3978`) makes an object whose function runs once after the collection that finds it unreachable: `garbage_collect` dooms the unmarked finalizers after the roots and before weak tables (`queue_doomed_finalizers`), keeps them and their functions, and calls each before it returns, with `inhibit-quit` t and a signal logged to *Messages* as `finalizer failed: ...` (`run_finalizers`, `alloc.c:3960`), automatic collections included. Its conservative stack scan may keep a finalizer a C frame still mentions.
rows.romacs: The collector dooms finalizers at GNU's point in marking and keeps them, with their functions, until they run (`crates/romacs-vm/src/gc.rs`). `romacs--run-finalizers` (`rlisp/vm/prelude.el`) calls them as `run_finalizers` does, from the engine just after an explicit `garbage-collect` returns its statistics, and before each wait for a command key (`romacs--timer-check-idle`): an automatic collection runs inside an allocation, where no Lisp may run, so its doomed finalizers wait for one of those. A finalizer a register of the running top-level evaluation still holds survives until that register is reused.
rows.why: Lisp cannot run inside an allocation. Test: `crates/romacs-vm/tests/garbage_collect.rs` (GNU-compared), `finalizer-object-type` in GNU's alloc-tests.el.

rows.gnu: `casetab.c:init_casetab_once` constructs four ASCII-only tables, subsequently enriched by GNU Lisp before the dumped oracle starts. The pinned dumped oracle maps character 192 to 224.
rows.romacs: Lazily constructs and independently roots all four ASCII startup tables and the canonical-to-equivalence link. Before the GNU enrichment runs, `(aref (standard-case-table) 192)` is nil, not the dumped oracle's 224.

rows.gnu: `src/data.c:531` accepts GNU closure objects with string bytecode; `#[0 "\\300\\207" [42] 1]` is one.
rows.romacs: `byte-code-function-p` is callable but returns nil for VM2's representable objects; the positive reader witness signals `invalid-read-syntax`. VM2 register-code closures are not GNU bytecode.
rows.why: GNU bytecode object representation, reader and producers are absent; this is a bounded negative-domain implementation, not bytecode execution support.

rows.gnu: `byte-compile` (`lisp/emacs-lisp/bytecomp.el:2959`) recovers an interpreted function's source through `byte-compile--reify-function` (`(aref fun 0..2)`), compiles it to byte-code and, for a symbol, `fset`s the result; a compiled function is returned with the message `Function %s is already compiled`. bytecomp.el itself byte-compiles seven of its functions when it is loaded from source
rows.romacs: Under the loadup bootstrap (`rlisp/romacs-bytecomp.el`, `:around` advice added before bytecomp.el loads) a VM2 closure, or a symbol whose definition is one, is returned unchanged and silently: VM2 compiled it when it was defined, and its closures are opaque (VM2-CLOSEQ1). A `(lambda ...)` list first goes through bytecomp's own front end (`byte-compile-preprocess`'s steps: `macroexpand-all`, then closure conversion as a check, inside GNU's `displaying-byte-compile-warnings`); when that signals, as for `(let 1)` or `(cond 1)`, the result is GNU's diagnostic string and nothing is `fset`. Otherwise its expansion, so each macro expands once, is evaluated in the dialect GNU would compile it in (a symbol's list definition dynamically, an argument in the caller's `lexical-binding`) and a symbol is `fset` to the closure. Other arguments and file compilation (`byte-compile-file`) reach GNU's code unchanged (`tests/bytecomp_function_value.rs`)
rows.why: **Package-observable:** the value is a VM2 closure, not byte-code: `byte-code-function-p` stays nil (VM2-BYTECODE1), so code that byte-compiles only when that predicate is nil (cc-defs.el:2517, cc-mode.el:490) calls `byte-compile` each time it is evaluated. An error GNU raises only in code generation, past the front end, is not reported for a list, and a VM2 closure is returned even when GNU's recompilation of its source would fail. `(advice-member-p #'romacs-bytecomp--function-value 'byte-compile)` is non-nil

rows.gnu: `admin/unidata/unidata-gen.el` byte-compiles its runtime functions into eight generated tables (`international/uni-name.el`, `uni-old-name.el`, `uni-comment.el`, `uni-decomposition.el`, `uni-category.el`, `uni-combining.el`, `uni-bidi.el`, `uni-brackets.el`): extra slots 1-3 of each `char-code-property-table` hold byte-code objects.

Every other generated `uni-*.el` file is the pinned build's bytes. Verified on all 1,114,112 code points in pinned GNU (`get-char-code-property` and `char-code-property-description` against stock tables), and on Romacs for 16 properties over U+0000-U+2FFFF.

rows.romacs: Every per-buffer slot plus ordinary locals, in symbol-slot order; details below.
rows.why: Romacs keeps locals by symbol, not in a native buffer structure.

A buffer replacement is `romacs--replace-range` (change hooks, undo, markers, match-data adjustment), then `upcase-region` or `upcase-initials-region` over the new text, then point after it. Conversion of initial letters shares VM2-CASE1 pinned titlecase limitations; a casing that expands a character follows VM2-CASE3. VM2 has no intangible text, so point always ends after the replacement.
rows.why: Buffer and string cases are compared with pinned GNU in `tests/replace_match.rs`.

rows.romacs: VM2's shared native arity dispatcher names the subr object; condition kind and argument count agree.

rows.gnu: GNU retains allocated unused match registers, including startup search history, and reports nonexistent subexpressions inside that capacity; a buffer replacement's `\N` past that capacity signals invalid replacement text and one inside it inserts nothing.

rows.mechanism: Calls of GNU's byte-op primitives are sealed: `car`, `cdr`, `cons`, `eq`, `memq`, `assq`, `nth`, `not`, `null`, `consp`, `listp`, `symbolp`, `stringp`, `length`, `aref`, `aset`, `setcar`, `setcdr`, `1+`, `1-`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `max`, `min`, `list`, `concat`, `insert`, `nconc`, `nreverse`, `get`, `set`, `fset`, `symbol-value`, `symbol-function`, `point`, `goto-char`, `char-after`, `set-buffer`, `current-buffer`, `equal`, `member`, `elt`, `nthcdr`, `substring`, `upcase`, `downcase`, `string=`, `string<`, the buffer and match primitives of `lisp/emacs-lisp/bytecomp.el:3970-4275` (`byte-defop-compiler` rows with an opcode), at the argument counts those handlers emit the opcode for (`crates/romacs-vm/src/sealed.rs` lists them; `sealed::tests` pins the list to the file).
rows.gnu: The byte compiler emits a byte code for such a call (`src/bytecode.c:658` `Bcar`, `:1083` `Bnot`, `:1331` `Bplus`, `:1675` `Bnconc`); byte code never reads the function cell, so *compiled* code ignores `fset`, `defalias`, `advice-add` and `cl-letf` of these names, while the *interpreter* (`eval_sub`) reads the cell and sees them. Cell readers (`funcall` of a variable holding the symbol, `apply`, `mapcar`, `symbol-function`) see them in both; byte-opt folds `(funcall 'car x)` and `(apply #'car (list x))` into the byte code. Pinned GNU 32.0.50 after `(advice-add 'car :around ADV)`: byte-compiled `(car '(1 2))` => `1`, `(funcall f '(1 2))` with `f` = `car` and `(mapcar #'car l)` => advised; interpreted `(car '(1 2))` => `(advised . 1)`. After `(fset '+ (lambda (a b) 'plus-redefined))`: compiled `(+ 8 3)` => `11`, interpreted => `plus-redefined`; `(defalias 'null ...)` leaves compiled `(null nil)` and `(not nil)` at `t`.
rows.romacs: Every call of these names compiles to the primitive itself (`Op::Sealed`), with no function-cell guard; `funcall`, `apply`, `mapcar` and `symbol-function` read the cell as in GNU, and `advice-add`/`advice-remove` on a sealed name work for them. Romacs has no interpreter: `eval`, `eval-expression`, `ielm` and `load` of source compile, so where GNU's interpreter would see a redefinition of `car`, Romacs behaves as GNU's compiled code. `(funcall 'car x)` is not folded and reads the cell (GNU compiled: the byte code). A call with an argument count GNU does not compile to a byte code (`(car a b)`, `(+ a b c)`, `(max)`) is an ordinary call and reads the cell. Rationale: a small set of primitives whose semantics cannot be changed is accepted Elisp practice (`bytecomp.el`'s own open-coding), and the per-call guard it replaces was 9% of `ert-tests.el`'s instructions and 2% of the GUI journey's; measurements in the commit. No `gnu-lisp/`, `rlisp/` or test code redefines a byte-op name except fixtures that probe the redefinition itself (`evidence/text-known-answers.json`, re-recorded from compiled GNU). Tests: `sealed::tests`, `tests/sealed_primitives.rs` (advice, against pinned compiled GNU), `tests/traversal.rs`, `tests/core.rs`.

rows.mechanism: Every named call compiled by Romacs (all Lisp is compiled: `eval`, `load`, `ielm`) evaluates its arguments, then reads the function cell.
rows.gnu: GNU's byte code does the same (`src/bytecode.c:758-829` `Bcall`: `call_args` are on the stack before `call_fun = XBARE_SYMBOL (call_fun)->u.s.function`); GNU's interpreter (`eval_sub`) reads the cell first. Pinned GNU 32.0.50, byte-compiled `(f (progn (fset 'f g) 1) 2)` calls `g`; `(undefined-fn (progn (setq zz 1) 2))` signals `void-function` with `zz` = 1; interpreted, `f` and no assignment.
rows.romacs: A redefinition, `advice-add` or `cl-letf` made while an argument runs is seen by that very call, and `void-function` for an unbound head is signalled after the arguments ran. A redefinition made before the call is always seen at the call (the site cache compares the cell's version on every call: `threaded.rs` `direct`, `direct_kernel`, `direct_generic`). One loader-order case is kept: a *top-level* form, or a form deferred to its reach (R215's non-eager regime), whose head has no function when it is compiled (typically a macro from a file not yet loaded) checks the head before its arguments, so a load stopping at `(define-inline …)` reports `(void-function define-inline)` as GNU's loader does, not the void variable its first argument would be; the check runs once per such form and never inside an eagerly compiled function body (there the void variable is reported first, as compiled GNU does).
rows.why: The compiled order is the one GNU packages are byte-compiled against; it costs one load-compare per call where the interpreter order needed a separate resolution instruction and a traced snapshot register per call (`named-call-1` micro and ERT/census measurements in the commit). Tests: `tests/call_heads.rs` `named_call_reads_the_cell_after_its_arguments`, `tests/oclosure.rs`.

rows.gnu: GNU `data.c:510` tests `PVEC_SUBR` (`lisp.h:2216`), including unevalled special-form subrs and native-compiled Lisp (`NATIVE_COMP_FUNCTIONP`, `lisp.h:5494`). Live pinned GNU reports `(subrp (symbol-function 'if))` and `(subrp (symbol-function 'get-upcase-table))` as t; the latter also satisfies `native-comp-function-p` and is defined in `lisp/case-table.el:84`, not C.

Each special form's function cell holds its subr, with arity `(MIN . unevalled)`, so `(subrp (symbol-function 'if))` is t as in GNU. There is no native-comp object kind or native library loader: the `get-upcase-table` witness returns nil and is pinned VALUE. `byte-compile` is GNU Lisp not loaded in the bare replay, pinned MISSING; compiled-function object introspection remains outside this implementation.

Never label VM2 bytecode closures native-comp subrs merely because the pinned binary native-compiles its Lisp libraries. `subrp/0052` is the inherited VM2-EV2 circular printer gap. Live evidence: `crates/romacs-vm/tools/primh/evidence/subrp.json`; object and alias tests: `tests/subrp_chain.rs`.

rows.gnu: GNU `data.c:362` tests the distinct `PVEC_SYMBOL_WITH_POS` object independent of `symbols-with-pos-enabled`; `position-symbol` and `read-positioning-symbols` construct it with a traced bare symbol and fixnum position (`lisp.h:957`, `lread.c:4254`). rows.romacs: VM2 has no positioned-symbol heap kind, reader mode or constructor; both producers remain void. Its predicate returns nil for every representable value, including all bare/uninterned symbols. No symbol property, cons or record is treated as this object.
rows.why: **Package-observable missing object substrate**, not full feature parity. Live pinned GNU `symbol-with-pos-p/0051`–`/0053` return `(ok t)`; VM2 reports missing producer (`MISSING` pins). Future producer/type additions must replace the nil predicate and its absence guard. The corpus's `/0060` is the inherited circular printer gap VM2-EV2, not predicate parity. rows.mechanism: Region casing that expands a character

rows.gnu: GNU `lread.c:2511` reads the complete Emacs syntax. `#s(` (`src/lread.c:3852`) opens a record; at `)` (`:3770-3780`) a first element `hash-table` makes a table through `hash_table_from_plist` (`:3153`: `test`, `weakness`, `purecopy` and `data` by `plist_get`, first pair wins; data must be a proper list of even length, checked before `make-hash-table`), any other first element a record via `record_from_list` (`:3198`); `#s` not followed by `(`, `#s()` and a dot token inside signal `invalid-read-syntax` with the buffered text (`"#sx"`, `"#s"`, `"."`). A `.` is the dot token only when the next character is a control/space character, NO-BREAK SPACE, one of `"';([#?` `` ` `` `,` or end of input (`:4126-4133`); before anything else, `)` and `]` included, it starts a symbol or number, so `#s(hash-table .)` reads `(#s(hash-table) . 16)` and `(a .)` is a list of `a` and the symbol `.`. A dot token outside a list with an element (list start, vector, record, top level, tail) signals `"."` (`:4140`); a closer in the tail position signals the closer (`:3789,3827`). Also `#N=`/`#N#`, the other `#` dispatch syntaxes, and raw unibyte strings (octet 255 remains unibyte)
rows.romacs: VM2 calls its actual source reader with character-index bounds and offsets. `#s(hash-table ...)` is read exactly as GNU, including its error conditions and data and its ignored keys (`crates/romacs-vm/src/reader.rs` `Reader::record`, `hash.rs` `hash_table_from_plist`; 108-case live-GNU corpus `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/hash-read-syntax/`, `tests/hash_read_syntax.rs`), so the `hashtable-print-readable` syntax is supported when reached (not a complete-subr load claim). Radix `#b`/`#o`/`#x`/`#Nr` syntax now has arbitrary-precision results and GNU-matched condition data (183 live pinned-GNU witnesses in `evidence/radix-reader/`). Records now have a distinct traced/forwarded heap representation and `#s(TYPE ...)` reads a record with GNU's 4095-total-slot limit (`tests/records.rs`). Remaining differences: (1) `#N=`/`#N#` labels are supported, self references included (`lread.c` read0's placeholder, then `substitute_object_recurse` through conses, vectors and records; `tests/numbered_references.rs`), and a quoted datum that contains itself is compiled as that object, as `quote` returns it; other unsupported dispatch syntaxes signal rather than fabricate objects; (2) a hash table read from SOURCE that is being compiled or loaded (a literal `#s(hash-table ...)` in code, as in `shortdoc-doc.el`) is a self-evaluating constant, as in GNU. `##`, `#:NAME`, `#_NAME` and `#!` read as GNU reads them. The dot rule is GNU's for lists, vectors and `#s(` alike (before vm2/hashread lists and vectors used VM2's general delimiter set, so `(a .?x)` and `(a .#s(hash-table))` read a symbol `.?x`/`.#s` and `(a .)`/`.)` were refused); its two remaining differences are VM2-READ2 (NO-BREAK SPACE after a dot) and VM2-READ5 (`"expected )"`). Raw and mixed 22-bit string input is now supported; non-Unicode symbol names explicitly signal, and other reader fault payloads remain partial
rows.why: **Package-observable staged reader:** circular and other dispatch round trips and source-literal hash tables still need reader substrate work.

rows.gnu: GNU `read_minibuf` (`src/minibuf.c:573`) runs a recursive command loop in ` *Minibuf-N*` shown in the selected minibuffer window; RET, C-j and C-g are bound in `minibuffer-local-map` by `lisp/minibuffer.el:3407-3415` to `exit-minibuffer` (`minibuffer.el:3077`) and `abort-minibuffers` (C, `minibuf.c:472`), whose `minibuffer-quit-recursive-edit` (`minibuffer.el:3104`) signals `minibuffer-quit`. `faces.el:2914` appends `face minibuffer-prompt` to the C value `(read-only t)` of `minibuffer-prompt-properties` (`minibuf.c:2697`). After the loop `add-to-history` (subr.el) records the input (`minibuf.c:1095`). In batch, without `executing-kbd-macro`, it reads stdin (`minibuf.c:653-661`)
rows.romacs: VM2 implements both DEFUNs through `defsubr!` (`src/prims/minibuf.rs`, T2) with GNU's argument checks and order, `string_to_object` and read-string's DEFAULT-VALUE rule in Rust, and the loop in Lisp (`src/prims/minibuf.el`, installed on first use). Supported: PROMPT, INITIAL-CONTENTS string or `(STRING . POSITION)`, KEYMAP, READ, HIST (unbound variable set to nil), DEFAULT-VALUE, INHERIT-INPUT-METHOD (accepted; no input methods exist). Different: (1) **input**: the command loop of VM2-KBD1 reads `unread-command-events` and then the executing keyboard macro while `executing-kbd-macro` is non-nil (GNU's batch prompt regime: `execute-kbd-macro`, `ert-simulate-keys`); otherwise VM2 is batch GNU with an empty stdin and signals `(end-of-file "Error reading from stdin")`, unless an embedder attached a host keyboard (the live GUI does: VM2-HOSTIN1), in which case keys are read from it as interactive GNU does; (2) **bootstrap stand-ins**: until GNU's `minibuffer.el` loads, the Lisp half defines minimal `exit-minibuffer` (no innermost-loop checks), `minibuffer-quit-recursive-edit` and `abort-minibuffers` (single level), and binds RET/C-j/C-g, only where nothing is defined or bound; (3) **prompt face**: VM2 starts from the C value, so the prompt has no `face minibuffer-prompt` until faces.el runs (pins `read-from-minibuffer/1747`, `/1751`, `/1752`); (4) **history**: recorded only if `add-to-history` is fbound, so a bare VM2 never updates `minibuffer-history` (pin `/1778`); while the prompt reads, `minibuffer-history-variable` is HIST's variable and `minibuffer-history-position` 0, so GNU's history commands work, but HISTPOS of `(HISTVAR . HISTPOS)` is dropped; (5) a character typed after propertied INITIAL-CONTENTS does not inherit its sticky properties, because VM2's `self-insert-command` does not inherit, so `minibuffer-allow-text-properties` returns them on INITIAL only (pin `/1755`); (6) the prompt's `read-only`/`field` properties are set but VM2 does not enforce read-only text, so DEL can delete into the prompt; (7) no `minibuffer-setup-hook` run unless `run-hooks` is fbound; as GNU, a minibuffer used before starts afresh (its overlays deleted, `minibuffer-mode` run when defined, the caller's directory, lines not truncated), `minibuffer-completing-file-name` is `lambda` inside a file-name read, and `minibuffer-exit-hook` runs through safe_run_hooks before the unwind; no completion-table rebinding or window-configuration restore; `yes-or-no-p` never uses a dialog box; when a command at the prompt deletes the calling window, VM2 leaves the minibuffer window selected instead of choosing another window (the level and `minibuffer-default` are still restored, test `deleting_the_calling_window_does_not_poison_later_prompts`); (8) recursive prompts follow `enable-recursive-minibuffers` but only the refusal path is evidenced
rows.why: **Package-observable**: (1) without a host keyboard, any prompt outside a keyboard-macro/`unread-command-events` context fails instead of waiting; (3)-(5) through text properties and `minibuffer-history`; (6) by deleting prompt text; (7) by hooks and introspection functions. Corpus: 2492 live-GNU cases (`tools/primh/evidence/read-from-minibuffer.json`, `read-string.json`), 5 pinned VALUE

rows.gnu: GNU's `command_loop_1`, `read_key_sequence` and `read_char` (`src/keyboard.c`) and `Fexecute_kbd_macro` (`src/macros.c:276`) are C. In batch with no unread event and no macro input left, `read_char` waits for the terminal indefinitely. `read_key_sequence` applies `input-decode-map`, `local-function-key-map`/`function-key-map` and `key-translation-map`, echoes keystrokes, runs `help-form` on the help character, and rewrites mouse down/drag events; `recent-keys` records every event shape
rows.romacs: VM2 runs them in Lisp (`rlisp/vm/keyboard.el`, installed with the minibuffer's half on first use) behind Rust entry points (`src/prims/keyboard.rs`), in GNU's order: hooks through `safe_run_hooks`, `command-execute`, `this-command-keys` bookkeeping, macro index and `kbd-macro-termination-hook`, `minibuffer-quit` only caught by the macro. Different: (1) with no unread event, no macro input and no host keyboard, a read signals `(end-of-file "Error reading from stdin")`, thrown out of the innermost recursive edit or minibuffer when there is one, instead of blocking; with SECONDS it returns nil at once and never waits on the host keyboard; (2) no echo, `help-form`, menus or down/drag rewriting; GNU's key translation maps (a pending prefix in any of them keeps the sequence open), unbound upper-case/shift fallback, mouse-area prefix keys, default bindings and remapping are kept, and `input-decode-map` and `local-function-key-map` are global rather than per terminal; (3) `recent-keys` records characters, symbol events and symbol commands only; (4) `read_char` takes `unread-post-input-method-events`, `unread-command-events` and `unread-input-method-events` in GNU's order, but no input method runs: `input-method-function` is never called; `input-pending-p` sees `unread-command-events` and the host keyboard, `discard-input` only the former; (5) without simple.el and subr.el (a bare VM) minimal `command-execute` and `undefined` stand in; (6) no point adjustment after a command, `delayed-warnings-hook` or PRIMARY selection update; macros are defined as macros.c and record_char define them (`start-kbd-macro`, `end-kbd-macro`, `call-last-kbd-macro`, `store-kbd-macro-event`, `cancel-kbd-macro-events`, `discard-input` ending the definition), each command's keys joining the macro once it ran without leaving a prefix argument, so kmacro.el's C-x (, C-x ), C-x e, F3 and F4 work (`harness/command_errors_live.py` against pinned GNU pgtk); (7) a wait for the host keyboard runs one timer_check pass per round and checks requeued input and SECONDS before it blocks, so a timer that reschedules itself at once delays neither a key nor SECONDS; pinned GNU, `-nw` and batch, reads the key but answers SECONDS only once the rescheduling stops
rows.why: **Package-observable** for code that reads past its macro input, relies on key translation or echo, or inspects recorded mouse events; (7) by `read-event` with SECONDS under such a timer, which returns on time. `crates/romacs-vm/tests/kbd_macro.rs`: 35 cases equal to pinned GNU batch and the end-of-input cases

rows.mechanism: Keyboard input read by a prompt in the middle of a command (GUI)
rows.gnu: GNU `read_char` (`src/keyboard.c`) first takes `unread-command-events`, then a keyboard macro, then redisplays (skipped while input is pending, `detect_input_pending`) and blocks in `wait_reading_process_output`; `read_minibuf`'s recursive edit runs inside the suspended command on the native stack, and redisplay may run Lisp (mode-line `:eval`). C-g typed while Lisp runs sets `quit-flag` asynchronously and interrupts it. Deleting the last frame runs `handle-delete-frame`/`save-buffers-kill-emacs`. RET is the function key `return`, translated to 13 by `function-key-map`
rows.romacs: Same order: the command loop's `romacs--read-char` (`rlisp/vm/keyboard.el`, VM2-KBD1) takes `unread-command-events`, then the executing macro, then calls `romacs--read-host-event`, engine control like `eval` (`threaded.rs` `reentrant_load`): the suspended register stack leaves the collector's view and collection is inhibited for the wait, redisplay (`Vm::frame_snapshot`, mode-line `:eval` included) runs in its own engine, the embedder (`Vm::set_host_input`, `host_input.rs`; the GUI's `prompt.rs`) paints and blocks on its input channel; pending input skips the redisplay. Different: (1) two internal names are visible: function `romacs--read-host-event` and variable `romacs--host-input` (t while a host is attached); (2) **no asynchronous quit**: C-g is an ordinary key, seen only when a prompt reads it, so it cannot interrupt running Lisp; (3) closing the frame while a prompt waits signals `quit` (catchable), from a recursive edit or minibuffer by leaving it first (as end of input does, VM2-KBD1), so the command loop there, which reports every signal, does not read again; every later read in that command signals `quit` again without waiting, and the GUI exits when the command returns, with no `delete-frame-functions` or kill-emacs query; (4) none for Return: the GUI delivers it as the function key `return` (`native.rs`), as GNU's X and pgtk frames do, and `local-function-key-map` makes an unbound one RET (13) both here and in the GUI's command loop (`command.rs`), so C-j stays 10; (5) keys read from the host are recorded as VM2-KBD1 records them; (6) between commands the GUI's loop (`crates/romacs-vm-gui/src/main.rs`) runs the Lisp command loop for one command whenever a host key arrives or a Lisp unread queue holds an event, so a key Lisp read and pushed back (sit-for in a timer) runs as the next command, read as read_char reads it (VM2-KBD1)
rows.why: **Package-observable**: (1) by `fboundp`/`boundp`; (2) by a long-running command (no `quit` arrives); (3) by `delete-frame-functions`/`kill-emacs-hook` not running; (5) as VM2-KBD1. Not observable: collection is deferred only for the duration of a wait (no Lisp allocates during it except redisplay's)

rows.romacs: Vertical tab is now handled exactly; hash and NBSP still remain part of ordinary symbol tokens. Only read-from-string/0163 and /0164 remain VALUE pins.

rows.gnu: GNU reads general signed decimal `N.NNe+INF` as infinity: `2.25e+INF` => `(1.0e+INF . 9)`, `-3.75e+INF` => `(-1.0e+INF . 10)`, both numeric.

rows.gnu: GNU reads a 257-level parenthesized zero at offset 515.
rows.romacs: VM2 signals `invalid-read-syntax` with `"reader nesting limit exceeded at byte 257"`: the source reader rejects depth >256; 256-level input succeeds at offset 513. Pin `read-from-string/0169` is `SIGNAL-VS-VALUE`; `/0173` is the successful lower-bound probe. Decimal integers past the fixnum range read as bignums, as GNU reads them.
rows.why: **Package-observable resource bound:** no nesting expansion in this slice; fail rather than recurse without bounds.

rows.gnu: Pinned GNU accepts `(+ #x2000000000000000 1)` => `2305843009213693953`, numeric `=`/`<=` of that integer with itself => t, and `(car (read-from-string (prin1-to-string #x2000000000000000)))` => the same integer.
rows.romacs: VM2 reads, prints and structurally compares radix bignums, but arithmetic, numeric comparison and min still reject them through the fixnum/float-only numeric consumers. The printed decimal spelling reads back as the same bignum. `%d` now accepts bignums and floating coercions (VM2-FMT1). Integerp/numberp returning t does not imply those consumers support the new representation.
rows.why: **Package-observable staged numeric consumers:** real arbitrary-precision reader storage, not general bignum arithmetic or serialization parity; reject rather than silently round.

rows.gnu: GNU reading `(a . b c)` signals `(invalid-read-syntax "expected )")`.
rows.romacs: VM2 signals `(invalid-read-syntax "dotted list requires one tail at byte 8")`; the same condition symbol does not imply matching condition data. `read-from-string/0170` is explicitly pinned `DATA`. Other reader errors may likewise expose internal messages/byte positions rather than GNU payloads.
rows.why: **Package-observable staged diagnostic contract:** preserve complete actual fault data in evidence rather than hide payload differences as printer behavior.

rows.gnu: GNU `search.c` retains signed match offsets; after `(set-match-data '(2 -1))`, `(match-string 0 "abcd")` returns `"c"` through substring's negative end normalization.
rows.romacs: VM2 stores offsets as unsigned internally; `match-data t` round-trips `(2 -1)`, but extraction rejects the wrapped end and signals `(args-out-of-range "abcd" 2 -1)`. `set-match-data/0507` is pinned `SIGNAL-VS-VALUE`, not a printer gap.
rows.why: **Package-observable bounded regexp state:** signed match state across every consumer needs separate substrate work; this slice documents safe range rejection rather than claim extraction parity.

rows.mechanism: `call-interactively`, `funcall-interactively`, `interactive-form`: the supported spec subset and what VM2 lacks around them
rows.gnu: GNU `Fcall_interactively` (`callint.c:256-801`) asks `interactive-form` through its symbol (`callint.c:305`), evaluates a non-string spec with `Feval` in the closure's lexical environment (`callint.c:316-319`), records on `command-history` through `add-to-history` (`callint.c:325-330`, `780-783`), handles the prefix characters `+ * - @ ^` (`callint.c:364-405`) and every code letter `a b B c C d D e f F G i k K m M n N p P r R s S U v x X z Z` (`callint.c:449-762`), formatting each prompt with `format-message` (`callint.c:457`). `Finteractive_form` (`data.c:1139-1210`) reads the `interactive-form` property along the alias chain, a subr's DEFUN intspec, `CLOSURE_INTERACTIVE`, autoloads (via `autoload-do-load`) and `(lambda ...)` lists. `funcall-interactively` (`callint.c:239-254`) is `Ffuncall` in a frame that `called-interactively-p` (subr.el) finds by walking the backtrace.
rows.romacs: Recorded live against GNU 32.0.50 through primh (`tools/primh/callint-specs/*.json`, `evidence/{call-interactively,funcall-interactively,interactive-form,prefix-numeric-value}.json`, inputs in `tools/primh/logs/callint/make_spec.py`). **Supported and matching GNU row-for-row:** prefix characters `* - ^ @` (`^` calls `handle-shift-selection` when it is fbound; `@` with a window event signals unsupported), `+` error, codes `d e i m p P r R U Z`(no prefix) `N`(with prefix), the reading codes `D f F G` (`read-file-name` through its symbol with callint.c's arguments) and `s` (the `read-string` subr, not its symbol), their prompts through `format-message` (`tests/callint_reading.rs`), invalid-letter error text, `this-command`/`this-original-command`/`real-this-command`/`last-command` save and restore, `current-prefix-arg` (never `prefix-arg`), KEYS vector and `inhibit-mouse-event-check`, RECORD-FLAG history items including `interactive-args`, `history-length` (variable and property), the list-spec path in the closure's own lexical environment, the `interactive-form` property chain, and the GNU intspecs of the VM2 subrs that GNU defines as commands. **Divergent:** (1) the other minibuffer/keyboard-reading codes (`a b B c C k K M n S v x X z`, `N` without and `Z` with a prefix) signals `(error "call-interactively: the input-reading code `X' is not supported in VM2 yet")` where GNU reads input (`call-interactively/0466`, `/0471` pinned `CONDITION`; GNU batch gives `end-of-file`); (2) a `%` in a prompt signals the same kind of unsupported error where GNU formats it (`/0497`, GNU `Not enough arguments for format string`); (3) VM2 has no mark, so `m`, `r` and an active-region `R` always take GNU's no-mark error, and `set-mark` is void (`/0475`); rows.mechanism: Lisp evaluation depth accounting and native stack exhaustion
rows.gnu: GNU eval.c:2604-2609,3196-3201 checks the dynamically bound integer limit (default 1600, floor 100 on overflow), signals `(excessive-lisp-nesting DEPTH)`, and restores depth on unwind; bytecode.c:783-788 signals plain `error` at compiled call overflow. loadup.el:106 raises the limit to 4200 and :156 doubles it. eval.c:255-277 restores borrowed reserve from CURRENT limit/reserve values; signal_or_quit borrows 20 (eval.c:1969). Per level at limit 100, measured at the pin: interpreted code reaches 30 `eval`-reentry and 45 call levels, byte-compiled 48 and 96. GNU has no recoverable native-stack condition (a C stack overflow is caught and Emacs returns to top level, `keyboard.c:166-169,13426` "Re-entering top level after C stack overflow")
rows.romacs: VM2 consults the forwarded limit at every Lisp activation and shares one budget across eval/load/macro engines; register storage grows and rebases; `eval`/load/lazy-compile/autoload reentry runs on heap stack segments grown on demand (`stacker`), so reentry depth is bounded by the Lisp counter, not by the thread stack. Separately (R193), every activation and every compiler `expr` step refuses when fewer than 256 KiB of native stack remain, with a recoverable `(error "native stack exhausted during Lisp evaluation")` or `... while compiling Lisp` (compiler recursion is refused, not grown). Accounting is GNU bytecode's: 50 and 99 levels at limit 100 (`tests/eval_depth.rs` `reentry_and_call_levels_follow_gnu_bytecode_accounting`). Measured sustainable depth (exactly 4200 and 8400 reached, then `excessive-lisp-nesting`): on the GUI evaluator's explicit 64 MiB stack for plain calls, `apply` and `run-hooks` recursion and `eval` reentry in debug, gate (optimized, no LTO) and release (LTO) builds; on a 2 MiB thread in debug and release for every shape. `signal-hook-function` borrows twenty levels from `lisp-eval-depth-reserve` (default 200), restoring on normal/error/throw exits
rows.why: **Package-observable:** (1) VM2 always signals `excessive-lisp-nesting`, also where GNU bytecode signals plain `error`; recursion reaches more levels than GNU's interpreter (50 vs 30, 99 vs 45). (2) as GNU's, the debugger borrows 200 levels (VM2-LEAF-DEBUG), and returning `handler-bind` callbacks borrow 200 levels and restore the current limit/reserve after normal or nonlocal exit. (3) In the gap between the native guard and the Lisp limit -- reached only on small threads in optimized non-LTO builds (2 MiB: `apply` recursion refused before depth 4200, `run-hooks` before 8400; 8 MiB: 8400 reached) or with a raised limit (50000 levels on 2 MiB) -- code sees a plain `error` with that message instead of `excessive-lisp-nesting`, and a handler for `excessive-lisp-nesting` alone does not catch it; it is never a process abort. GNU's 4200/8400 loadup raises are effective at the GUI's 64 MiB. See `src/eval_depth.rs` and `tests/eval_depth.rs`.

rows.gnu: `romacs FILE` and the desktop entry's `%F` visit FILE with `find-file` (startup.el `command-line-1`, files.el); GNU `find-buffer-visiting` checks expanded name, truename and revalidated file identifier. `C-x C-s` runs `save-buffer`, which makes backups, runs save hooks, checks visited modtime, routes conflicts through `ask-user-about-supersession-threat`, and clears modified state. GNU `kill-buffer` runs query functions, aborts on nil, runs the kill hook, detaches the buffer and repairs windows. Modification state compares SAVE_MODIFF with MODIFF, not text; real undo may explicitly restore clean via saved-modtime undo metadata
rows.romacs: While GNU files.el is unavailable the GUI uses explicitly named romacs adapters over native primitives. `romacs-gui-visit-file` uses native exact-name, saved-truename and revalidated device/inode identity, reusing hardlinks, symlinks, equivalent paths and direct Lisp native visits without losing edits. Failed GUI visits are cleared/killed rather than adopted as successful empty buffers. Startup consumes `+LINE[:COLUMN]` and `--`. Save is a no-op when native `buffer-modified-p` is nil; otherwise native stat-only `verify-visited-file-modtime` checks nanosecond time and recorded size, without disk-content reads. Conflicts install future-key y/n/C-g overwrite confirmation: y writes and refreshes metadata; n/C-g preserve both versions. Same modtime/size content changes are deliberately not interrogated, matching GNU. Removed files also prompt here, unlike GNU recreation policy. A dynamic mode-line `*`/`-` reflects native modification counters, including inverse edits to saved bytes. Existing GNU mode-line-format is preserved. In the workspace without GNU Lisp (with it, C-x k is GNU's `kill-buffer`, which asks before killing a modified file buffer), C-x k now truly kills the captured buffer after y (clean buffers immediately), runs native query/hook lifecycle and honors vetoes; dead identities remain buffer objects, leave registries, detach markers/overlays and are replaced in windows. C-x C-c/native close confirm modified GUI visits, including hidden visits. Non-answer/prefix input or buffer switch cancels pending consent instead of GNU modal reprompting; GUI confirmation is an asynchronous adapter, not GNU userlock.el. Native kill lacks process/indirect/autosave/lock/update-hook lifecycle and GNU window-history policy (see crates/romacs-vm/GNU-DIVERGENCES.md). Native alias lookup is named `romacs-find-buffer-visiting`, not full GNU `find-buffer-visiting` predicate/handler support; noncurrent anonymous visits are not enumerated. No native undo record/replay, backups or save hooks; the save reports the write's GNU `Wrote` message. GNU display-column customization/ctl-arrow/C1 controls are not fully implemented for startup positions
rows.why: **User-observable and package-observable**: ordinary supersession, confirmed/vetoed kill, hardlink reuse and counter-based modified indication are implemented. Packages can call native get-file-buffer, modified-state and kill primitives, but do not acquire GNU save-buffer/find-file/userlock/undo Lisp through these adapters. Exact timestamp, callback-list mutation, omitted kill subsystems and alias lookup limits remain observable. A reverse edit remains modified; a real GNU undo-to-save may become clean and cannot yet run in VM2. FIFO no-reader/deadline behavior remains a deliberate divergence described in VM2-FILEIO1.

rows.gnu: `load` of a `.el` file goes through `load-source-file-function` (`load-with-code-conversion`, `lisp/international/mule.el`): `insert-file-contents` decodes it by the `coding:` cookie or, without one, by `set-auto-coding` and the detection walk over `coding-system-priority-list` (pinned GNU batch: a file of valid UTF-8 is `utf-8`, `caf\xe9` is `iso-latin-1`, `x\x85y` is `japanese-shift-jis`, and `leim/quail/Punct.el`, whose comment holds two stray GB2312 bytes, is `raw-text`, so its strings read as unibyte bytes). rows.gnu: Every zero-length string is one of two shared objects and every zero-length vector is `zero_vector` (`src/alloc.c:2329-2330,2358-2359,2903,3424`): `(eq "" "")`, `(eq (copy-sequence "") "")`, `(eq (vector) [])` and `(eq (substring "abc" 3) "")` are all t, and `(substring "" nil nil)` returns its argument.
rows.romacs: VM2 allocates a fresh object for each empty string or vector, so all of those are nil.
