rows.mechanism: `format` never returns its format string itself
rows.gnu: When formatting produces no change, `styled_format` returns the FORMAT argument itself (`src/editfns.c:4301-4304` at pin `45b0f7699df`, `if (! new_result) { val = args[0]; ...}`): `(let ((s (copy-sequence "abc"))) (list (eq (format "%s" s) s) (eq (format s) s) (eq (format "%s" "") "")))` is `(t t t)` on GNU 32.0.50.
rows.romacs: VM2's `format` always allocates a fresh string: the same form is `(nil nil nil)` (measured, `romacs-vm --eval-stream`, lane `vm2/bulk1`). `string-trim` and `string-replace` share GNU's no-change identity but are void in VM2 today, so they are not yet a divergence.
rows.why: **Package-observable identity only:** code that tests `(eq (format ...) s)` to detect "nothing changed", or that mutates the result expecting to leave the argument intact (GNU would mutate the argument), behaves differently. Contents and properties match. Not fixed in the `core` batch, which does not touch `format`; recorded because it was known and unrecorded.

rows.mechanism: a closure is not a sequence in VM2
rows.gnu: A closure is a vector-like object in GNU 32.0.50, so `length`, `append` and `mapcar` accept it as a sequence: `(length (lambda (x) x))` is 5 for the byte-compiled closure and 3 for the interpreted one (both regimes recorded; `src/fns.c:154` at pin `45b0f7699df`, `Flength` counts a `CLOSUREP` object's slots).
rows.romacs: Ordinary VM2 closures remain opaque objects: all three signal `wrong-type-argument`. Explicit `make-interpreted-closure` values and marked OClosures expose their supported metadata slots; this does not make ordinary closures sequences. `aref` of slot 2, the environment, answers for a closure made where no lexical binding is visible (a top-level `defun` or `lambda`): GNU's is then the dialect's alone, `(t)` or nil, which nadvice reads to run an advised command's computed interactive form (`tests/closure_environment.rs`); under a `let` it still signals, as do slots 0 and 1. Pinned in the bulk `core` corpus as `length/0071`, `append/1041`, `mapcar/0257` (class `VALUE`; the probes catch the type error as -99 so the closure is never printed).
rows.why: **Package-observable, rarely:** only code that measures or walks a function object's slots (OClosure internals, some debuggers/`cl-print`) sees the difference. General closure sequence operations remain out of scope. OClosure uses the explicit metadata boundary described in VM2-OCLOSURE1.

rows.mechanism: calling a symbol whose cell is a macro: `invalid-function` without data
rows.gnu: `funcall`/`apply` of a symbol whose function cell is a macro signals `(invalid-function SYMBOL)` (`src/eval.c` `funcall_general`): `(progn (fset 'q '(macro . car)) (condition-case e (funcall 'q 1) (error e)))` and the same through `(assoc 2 '((1 . a)) 'q)` both give `(invalid-function q)` on GNU 32.0.50.
rows.romacs: VM2 refuses the call with the text fault "invalid function: macro is not callable" (`crates/romacs-vm/src/threaded.rs` `invoke_full`, `t2_resolve`), so the condition is `invalid-function` with NO data: `(invalid-function)`. Funcalling the literal `(macro . car)` matches GNU. Pre-existing (present at `0aded923`); found by the second Sol review of `vm2/bulk1`, not changed by it.
rows.why: **Package-observable data only:** handlers that dispatch on `invalid-function` still catch it; code reading `(cadr e)` to name the offending function sees nothing.

rows.gnu: Both are C subrs (`src/keymap.c:2010`, `src/keymap.c:646`), and `where-is-internal` walks `Faccessible_keymaps` in C. `get_keyelt` follows a circular `(STRING . DEFN)` or `menu-item` wrapper forever
rows.romacs: VM2 defines both in its built-in prelude (`rlisp/vm/prelude.el`), since the walk calls `map-keymap`'s Lisp callback (PRIMITIVE-DOCTRINE section 3); `where-is-internal` walks `accessible-keymaps` as GNU's does. Their values, order, cycle rule, meta-prefix folding, string prefixes and `:filter` application match pinned GNU (`tests/journey_primitives.rs`); a circular wrapper signals `Circular menu item`
rows.why: **Package-observable metadata:** `subrp` of either is nil and their arity errors are a closure's, as for `mapcar` (VM2-MAPCAR1)

rows.gnu: Both are C subrs over lread.c's `readevalloop`, which `load` also uses (through `load-with-code-conversion`): `load` of a source file binds `eval-buffer-list` to its reading buffer
rows.romacs: VM2 defines both in its built-in prelude (`rlisp/vm/prelude.el`) over one Lisp `readevalloop`: GNU's dialect choice (the file's cookie, then `internal--get-default-lexical-binding-function`), eager expansion through `internal-macroexpand-for-load` with a `progn`'s forms taken one at a time, a top-level `(defvar NAME)` special for the later forms (passed as `eval`'s environment, as Fdefvar extends GNU's), READ-FUNCTION and `load-read-function`, PRINTFLAG streams and `values`, narrowing, `eval-buffer-list` and `load-history` (`tests/journey_primitives.rs`). `load` stays VM2's Rust loader, which reads the file's bytes and binds no reading buffer, so `eval-buffer-list` is nil while a file loads. A partial `eval-region` merges every new definition into an existing `load-history` entry; GNU's build_load_history keeps only the last
rows.why: **Package-observable metadata:** `subrp` of either is nil and their arity errors are a closure's (VM2-MAPCAR1); code that inspects `eval-buffer-list` during `load` sees it empty

rows.mechanism: Compile-time requires of source-loaded GNU Lisp
rows.gnu: GNU loads its bundled Lisp as `.elc`, where an `(eval-when-compile (require 'X))` left nothing: X loads only if something else needs it. So eshell's `esh-util.el` (and `term.el`) do not load `ange-ftp`
rows.romacs: VM2 loads that Lisp from source and compiles each function when it is defined, so macros from X must exist then: the `require` runs, and X's load-time effects happen. Requiring `esh-util`, as `eshell` and `project-eshell` (`C-x p e`) do, loads `ange-ftp`, which adds `ange-ftp-set-buffer-mode` to `find-file-hook`; it tests each visited name with `posix-string-match` and changes nothing for a local file. Skipping such requires is unsound while a function body cannot pick up a macro defined after the body was compiled (GNU's evaluator expands it when the call is evaluated; VM2 signals `invalid-function`)
rows.why: **Package-observable:** `(featurep 'ange-ftp)` and `find-file-hook` differ after eshell loads; visiting behaves as GNU's. File-name completion (`~/` typed in the middle of a path, `~USER`) loads neither tramp nor ange-ftp, as in GNU (`tests/journey_primitives.rs`)

rows.mechanism: `mapcar` is a Lisp function in VM2
rows.gnu: `mapcar` is the C subr `Fmapcar` (`src/fns.c:3551`, arity `(2 . 2)`): `(subrp (symbol-function 'mapcar))` is t, and a wrong argument count signals `(wrong-number-of-arguments #<subr mapcar> N)`.
rows.romacs: VM2 defines `mapcar` in its built-in prelude (`crates/romacs-vm/src/prims/prelude.el`) because a Rust primitive must not call Lisp from a loop (GC doctrine): `subrp` of it is nil, `symbol-function` returns a closure, and a wrong count signals the compiled-closure form `(wrong-number-of-arguments (2 . 2) N)`. Its traversal, element order, length-first checking, shortening by the callback and its signals match GNU case for case on the bulk `core` corpus, except the four arity rows `mapcar/0203`-`0206` (pinned `DATA`) and a closure used as the SEQUENCE (`mapcar/0257`, VM2-CLOSEQ1).
rows.why: **Package-observable metadata:** code inspecting `subrp`/`subr-arity` of `mapcar`, or reading the function datum of its arity error, sees a closure. Ordinary calls over lists, vectors, strings and bool-vectors are indistinguishable.

rows.mechanism: `defcustom` stores the raw default form where GNU stores a thunk, and `:set` is never invoked
rows.gnu: Measured on GNU 32.0.50 for `(defcustom e-opt (progn (setq n (1+ n)) 7) "d" :type 'integer)`: `(get 'e-opt 'standard-value)` is `((funcall #'#[nil ((progn (setq n (1+ n)) 7)) (t)]))` — a list whose car is a **form that calls a closure** wrapping the default — so `(eval (car (get 'e-opt 'standard-value)) t)` returns `7` and re-runs the side effect. A `:set` function runs **once at definition**. `custom-variable-p` answers non-nil
rows.romacs: VM2 stores the **raw unevaluated form**: `standard-value` is `((progn (setq n (1+ n)) 7))`. `(eval (car (get 'e-opt 'standard-value)) t)` **signals `void or non-function`** rather than returning 7, and the side effect does not re-run. A `:set` function is recorded under `custom-set` but **never invoked** — the setter counter stays 0 where GNU's reaches 1. `custom-type` and the other keyword properties match GNU, and **`custom-variable-p` matches GNU exactly** (`t` for a `defcustom`-defined symbol, `nil` otherwise). No theme machinery (removed by R90)
rows.why: **Package-observable** in two ways. Code that recomputes a default via `(eval (car (get 'sym 'standard-value)) t)` — which is what Custom itself does — gets an error instead of the value. Code relying on `:set` running at definition time silently does not get its setter called, so a variable whose setter has side effects beyond `set-default` is left uninitialised. Ordinary reads of the variable's value are identical, and `custom-variable-p` is not a difference. Revertible: wrap the stored form so `eval` of the car yields the default, and invoke `custom-set` at definition

rows.mechanism: A local `(defvar x)` reaches `let` but not lambda parameters
rows.gnu: GNU's `funcall_lambda` (`src/eval.c:3433`) binds arguments by consing onto `lexenv` whenever `lexenv` is non-nil and **never** consults a local-special marker, while `Flet`/`FletX` (`eval.c:1109`, `:1183`) check `declared_special` and `Fmemq (var, Vinternal_interpreter_environment)`. A one-argument `Fdefvar` enters the interpreter environment only
rows.romacs: VM2 matches GNU: the compiler's parameter-binding path does not consult local specials, while its `let` path does. Verified on live GNU 32.0.50 interpreted with `lexical-binding: t` on line 1 — the lambda-parameter form signals `void-variable`, the `let` form answers 18
rows.why: **Not a divergence in behaviour**; recorded because VM2 briefly implemented the symmetric (wrong) rule and a reader may expect symmetry. Both directions are pinned by `local_declaration_does_not_reach_lambda_parameters_but_does_reach_let` and mutation-proven

rows.mechanism: A globally special name binds lambda parameters dynamically
rows.gnu: GNU's `funcall_lambda` (`src/eval.c:3433-3436`) binds every parameter of a lexical closure by consing onto `lexenv` whenever `lexenv` is non-nil, without consulting `declared_special`; the byte compiler also binds such a parameter lexically. Live GNU 32.0.50 over `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/file-local-special/flr.el` (`(defvar flp-x 0)`, then `(funcall (lambda (flp-x) (flp-get)) 42)` where `flp-get` reads the dynamic value): `(0 43)` interpreted and `(0 43)` byte-compiled (`gnu-cache-kinds.txt`)
rows.romacs: VM2's compiler binds a parameter dynamically when its name is globally special (`declare_special`/`defvar` with a value), so the same fixture answers `(42 43)` (`vm2-af1209d0-probes.txt`): the callee sees the argument instead of the global value. `let` matches GNU (dynamic)
rows.why: **Package-observable** for code that names a lambda or `defun` parameter after a global special variable (the byte compiler warns about it) and relies on callees NOT seeing the argument; found while reviewing VM2-FILESPECIAL1's cache key, which now records global and file-local declarations separately because they compile differently. Revertible by binding parameters lexically regardless of global specialness in the compiler's parameter path

rows.mechanism: A file-local `(defvar x)` reaches the rest of its file only when it is a bare top-level form
rows.gnu: `Fdefvar` with one argument (`src/eval.c:990-996`) conses SYMBOL onto `internal-interpreter-environment` when that is non-nil; `readevalloop` (`src/lread.c`) binds the variable once for the whole file and evaluates each form with `eval_sub`, which does not rebind it, so the declaration makes SYMBOL dynamically bound by every LATER `let` and closure of that file and of no other file. A `progn`, `when` or binding-less `let` around it does not rebind the environment either, so `(progn (defvar x))`, `(when t (defvar x))` and `(let () (defvar x))` at top level all persist; `(when nil (defvar x))` does not run and declares nothing. Live GNU 32.0.50: `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/file-local-special/` (`gnu-transcript.txt`, `nested-forms.txt`)
rows.romacs: VM2's loader records a top-level form that is exactly `(defvar SYMBOL)` once it has evaluated, and seeds the root compilation of every later form of the same file with those names (`crates/romacs-vm/src/loader.rs`); it also conses the name onto the file's binding of `macroexp--dynvars`, as GNU's `macroexpand--all-toplevel` does, so a macro that evaluates code at expansion time (`eval-and-compile` inside `pcase-defmacro`) hands the declaration to `eval`, saving and restoring the set around each `load`; the source cache keys its validity on them, so an identical form in a file without the declaration is recompiled. A declaration nested inside a top-level `progn`/`when`/`let` still reaches only the rest of its own form (the compiler's existing local-special scope, VM2-VD1), so GNU's `(1 2 3 unbound)` for the four nested shapes above is VM2's `(unbound unbound unbound unbound)` past the form. `eval-buffer`/`eval-region` are not covered. Before this row (fixed on `vm2/defvar-local`) even the bare form reached nothing past itself, which made cl-macs.el's `(defvar cl--loop-args)` (line 939) ineffective. The source caches (in memory and persistent) key a cached form on each name's declaration KIND, lexical / file-local / global (`Vm::special_kind`), and the persistent cache's portable compiler reproduces file-local declarations as file-local (Sol review of af1209d0: it had made them global, so a warm load bound a lambda parameter dynamically where the cold load bound it lexically; `tests/file_local_special.rs`). Also different, pre-existing and not introduced by this row's fix (measured by that review, `evidence/file-local-special/fld.el`, `gnu-cache-kinds.txt`): `(defvar nil)` and `(defvar t)` signal `cannot declare a constant` where GNU returns `nil` and `t`; `(special-variable-p 'nil)` and `(special-variable-p 't)` are nil where GNU answers t; and a one-argument `(defvar x)` executed inside a function that is called at top level declares nothing for later forms, where GNU's later `let` binds x dynamically (fixture: GNU `(t t 9 7)`, VM2 `(nil nil 9 unbound)`)
rows.why: **Package-observable** for files that declare a variable special inside a wrapping top-level form and bind it in later forms; the bare `(defvar x)` that cl-macs.el and most of `lisp/` use behaves as GNU

rows.mechanism: VM2 keymap skeleton is installed lazily
rows.gnu: GNU builds `global-map`, `esc-map`, `ctl-x-map`, `function-key-map`, `key-translation-map` and `special-event-map` while loading `lisp/subr.el` and `lisp/bindings.el`, so by the time any user Lisp runs these variables are already bound to keymaps (`src/keymap.c:syms_of_keymap` defines the variables; the maps themselves come from Lisp)
rows.romacs: VM2 boots without loading `subr.el` and installs the same skeleton on **first use of any keymap primitive** rather than in `Vm::new`. Reading `global-map` (or the other five) before calling any keymap primitive signals `void-variable`, where GNU returns a keymap; after any keymap primitive runs, the variables are bound and behave as GNU
rows.why: **Package-observable** only by Lisp that reads one of these six variables without first calling a keymap function, which `bindings.el` and ordinary configuration do not do. Chosen so a freshly constructed VM allocates nothing: the collector's tests assert exact heap contents and arena indices, and a constructor-time skeleton silently redefines "empty heap" for all of them. Revertible by calling `initialize_keymaps` from `Vm::new` and converting those GC tests to arena-relative indices

rows.gnu: `keyboard.c:command_loop_1/read_key_sequence` accumulate prefixes, translate events, invoke hooks and call `call-interactively` (`callint.c:Fcall_interactively`) on the binding

The live GUI does not use it: each command runs through the Lisp command loop's one-step entry (`romacs--run-host-command`, rlisp/vm/keyboard.el `romacs--host-command`, keyboard.c command_loop_2/command_loop_1), whose reader takes the unread queues, a keyboard macro, then host keys, applies `input-decode-map`, `local-function-key-map` and `key-translation-map` (VM2-KBD1), and runs `pre-command-hook` and `post-command-hook` around each command, also after one that signalled. `interactive` evaluated as a form returns nil

rows.mechanism: GUI command-loop errors in the echo area
rows.gnu: `keyboard.c` `command-error-default-function` prints the error with `print_error_message` into the echo area and rings the bell; `command_loop_1` clears the echo area when the next command starts. `call-interactively` of a key bound to a symbol with no function signals `(wrong-type-argument commandp SYMBOL)` (GNU 32.0.50: `Wrong type argument: commandp, romacs-nonexistent-cmd`)
rows.romacs: The GUI host echoes `error-message-string` of the error rebuilt from VM2's printed condition and data, clears it when the next non-prefix command starts, and rings the bell. A command that returns normally leaves its last message (`message`, or printing to `t`) in the echo area, without its text properties. Data that cannot be re-read (`#<buffer x>`) falls back to `CONDITION: DATA`. VM2's `call-interactively` of a void command signals `(wrong-type-argument)` with no data, so `M-x` under `--gnu-lisp` shows `Wrong type argument` where GNU shows `Wrong type argument: commandp, execute-extended-command`. Unbound keys only ring the bell: GNU's `KEYS is undefined` needs C `key-description`, which VM2 lacks
rows.why: **User-observable** echo text; the void-command signal data is Lisp-visible through `condition-case` (a VM2 divergence, surfaced here, not introduced)

rows.gnu: `keyboard.c:make_lispy_event` and live GNU 32.0.50 `(kbd "C-SPC")` yield `[67108896]`, while C-@ is zero

rows.mechanism: Raw bytes (eight-bit characters #x3FFF80..#x3FFFFF) in multibyte buffers

rows.mechanism: `replace-region-contents` past MAX-SECS with a vector SOURCE

rows.gnu: process.c and callproc.c: process objects (`make-process`, `make-pipe-process`, `make-network-process` for every socket kind, `make-serial-process`), filters and sentinels run by `wait_reading_process_output` in every wait (`accept-process-output`, `sleep-for`, `sit-for`, and the command loop's idle wait), which also runs ordinary and idle timers (keyboard.c `timer_check`); SIGCHLD wakes the wait; `call-process` reads its output incrementally, with DISPLAY redisplaying
rows.romacs: Process objects, `make-process` (pipes or a pty), `make-pipe-process`, `call-process`, `call-process-region`, signals, filters, sentinels and the wait are GNU's transcribed (`crates/romacs-vm/src/subprocess.rs`, `prims/process.rs`, `rlisp/vm/subprocess.el`). Limits, each an explicit refusal or a stated difference: `make-network-process` makes TCP stream servers and clients only, refusing datagrams, local sockets, `:local`/`:remote` addresses, numeric families, non-numeric service names, `:tls-parameters` and `:use-external-socket`; a `:nowait` client connects without blocking and the wait reports its outcome (the `open` sentinel or `failed`, after trying each further address) as GNU does; `make-serial-process`, `process-attributes`, `list-system-processes`, `set-process-thread` and the datagram functions are void. Lisp waits never read the keyboard. Timers are keyboard.c's `timer_check` in Lisp (`rlisp/vm/subprocess.el`), shared by those waits, the GUI host's command loop and its key reads (prompts, and `read-event` with a time limit, hence `sit-for`): ordinary timers run as they fall due; while the GUI waits idle for a key (`timer_start_idle` until the next key press, `timer_stop_idle`), idle timers run too and `current-idle-time` is the idle duration; Lisp a command runs is never idle, so its waits run idle timers only inside a timer that itself runs while idle, as GNU's. The command loop's idle wait and the host's key reads (`romacs--read-host-char`) also read the processes' ready output, finish their connections and report their status changes (`romacs--process-idle`), as read_char's wait_reading_process_output does with the keyboard; the command loop redisplays after any timer ran or process output came and otherwise blocks until the next timer, key, ready process descriptor (`Vm::process_wait_fds`, `ProcessWatch`) or native wake. `make-network-process` is provided with the subfeatures it supports: `(:server t)`, `(:service t)`, `(:family ipv6)`, `(:family ipv4)` and `(:nowait t)`. `call-process` reads all output before inserting it, so DISPLAY never redisplays; a quit does not kill its child. Exited children are found by a polled `waitpid` and pidfds, not SIGCHLD; children a dropped VM leaves are reaped by the host's one shared reaper thread where GNU's exit leaves them to init. Process output is decoded per VM2-PROC2

rows.mechanism: `eval` and macro expansions copy list structure into source
rows.gnu: GNU `Feval` (`src/eval.c:2548`) evaluates the datum itself, and a macro's expansion is evaluated as the object it returned: quoted objects anywhere in it are `eq` to the originals, any object (closures, buffers) may appear in it — `(eval (list (lambda (x) (* x 2)) 21) t)` => 42, `eval-when-compile` (byte-run.el:674) may return a list holding a closure — a circular form is only walked as far as evaluation goes, and bare symbols in a LEXICAL alist mark local specials
rows.romacs: A non-symbol atom, a top-level `(quote X)` and an alist-bound symbol return the identical object, and a non-symbol head or dotted argument list is diagnosed on the datum before conversion, as GNU does. Any other form, and every macro expansion, is converted to compiler source. Objects with no source spelling (closures, primitives, buffers, markers, hash tables, ...) are now carried as themselves, in `eval` data, macro expansions and lazily held bodies: they evaluate to themselves, are `eq` to the originals when quoted, and a closure or primitive in head position is called, as GNU does (this closed the `source datum required` limit that stopped macroexp.el:955; pin `eval/0509` removed). In `eval`, every `(quote X)` in the datum, and every alist value, is the identical object, so a form that rewrites the structure it quotes, as esh-cmd.el's `eshell-do-eval` does to record its progress, sees its own rewrite. Still different: in macro expansions, and outside `quote` in an `eval` datum, list cells, strings, vectors and floats are copied, so they are not `eq` to the originals (`(eq L (eval-when-compile L))` is nil, GNU t); circular forms signal `circular-list`; alist entries become fresh `let` bindings (not shared with the alist); a bare alist symbol is locally special for the form and its closures, as a file's `(defvar NAME)` is (VM2-FILESPECIAL1), so only `let` binds it dynamically, while an alist binding of the same name stays lexical and is what references read; a circular or dotted alist signals only for a symbol form, as GNU's `assq` would, while other forms then evaluate without it. LEXICAL nil compiles every binding dynamically
rows.why: **Package-observable identity limits:** code that relies on `eq` of list, string or vector structure spliced into an `eval`ed form or a macro expansion (or mutates such a quoted constant expecting the original to change) differs. Splicing live objects (closures, buffers) now behaves as in GNU. The harness pins 8 printer rows (circular data) and 2 arity-data rows

A datum holding an object with no spelling compiles for each use. Copied constants (VM2-EVAL2) are therefore created once and shared by every evaluation of that structure, as GNU shares the datum's own objects

rows.mechanism: Variable watchers of native writes run with collection held
rows.gnu: `add-variable-watcher` (`src/data.c:1857`) accepts any function; `notify_variable_watchers` calls it before every `set`, `let`, `unlet`, `makunbound` and `defvaralias` of the variable, with WHERE the buffer of a buffer-local binding

Bindings follow `specbind`/`do_one_unbind`: a `let` records the binding before its watchers run; restoring a localized or per-buffer default binding, or binding a per-buffer default, reports `set` with WHERE nil; restoring a global forwarded variable reports `set` then `unlet`, and its `set-default` reports twice; restoring a killed local, and `kill-local-variable` of a forwarded variable, report nothing. A native leaf subr runs in place; any other watcher is funcalled at the write point. A write from compiled code (`setq`, `let`, a `(lambda ...)` list's parameters, their unbinding) suspends its engine and roots the value, so the watcher may collect; a native writer's watchers (`set`, `set-default`, `defvaralias`, `kill-local-variable`, a load's own bindings) run with collection held until they return, because that writer's locals are not rooted (`tests/variable_watchers.rs`, `tests/gc_reentry.rs`, VM2-GC-INHIBITED). A failed load is undone by `un_autoload` (`src/eval.c:2447`), which re-reads each redefined symbol's previous definition from its `function-history` property (`add_to_function_history`, `src/data.c:933-967`, which keeps one entry per file); `defalias` also honours `defalias-fset-function` and records `load-history`; the "failed to define" error names `(car (car load-history))`, the file as `openp` found it
rows.romacs: Since `vm2/autoload`, calls, `funcall`, `apply`, call requests from primitives (`Step::Call`) and the compiler's macro expansion load the file exactly as GNU (macro expansion now also follows symbol aliases to a macro or macro autoload, as `Fmacroexpand` does at `src/eval.c:1290-1305`; before this lane an alias of a macro compiled as a function call), `autoload-do-load` (1 . 3) matches GNU's argument contract, a failing load reverts function cells and `features` and keeps functions that had no previous definition, nested loads undo only their own level, `require` shares the undo, and match data is saved (`crates/romacs-vm/src/autoload.rs`, tests `tests/autoload_load.rs`, GNU transcript `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/autoload-load/gnu-transcript.txt`; primh row `autoload/0497` now matches and is unpinned). Remaining: (1) VM2 has no `function-history`, so the undo record is the old definition captured at `defalias` time; GNU's re-read differs only if Lisp edits that property mid-load or the same file redefines a symbol it defined on an earlier load; (2) keymap, `interactive-form` and command-loop autoloads are not loaded (VM2 `get_keymap` returns None for an autoload); (3) no `load-history`, so the "Autoloading file %s failed to define function %s" message names the canonicalized path VM2 loaded; (4) `defalias-fset-function` is not honoured; (5) VM2 macroexpands when it compiles the whole top-level form, so a failing macro autoload fails that form's compilation instead of signalling where the call is reached (an enclosing `condition-case` in the same form cannot catch it; see VM2-LAZY4)
rows.why: **Package-observable** for autoloaded keymaps and commands invoked through the command loop before their file is loaded, for code inspecting `function-history`/`load-history`, and through symlinked load paths in the error text. Calling or expanding an autoloaded function or macro behaves as in GNU

rows.mechanism: Symbol property lists: the condition projections, `overriding-plist-environment`, VM-internal command specs, image plists
rows.gnu: GNU stores one plist per symbol object (`u.s.plist`, `src/lisp.h`; marked with the symbol, `src/alloc.c:6673`). `get` first consults `overriding-plist-environment` (`src/fns.c:2653-2663`); `put` is `plist_put` (`src/fns.c:2703-2741`). `symbol-plist` shows every property, including the `error-conditions`/`error-message` that `define-error` puts (live: `((error-conditions (#:c error) error-message "Made") "Made")`), a condition defined only by `setplist` reports its own message (live: `(caught #:c "C!: 1")`), and `(let ((overriding-plist-environment '((foo p 9)))) (get 'foo 'p))` is `9`. Transcripts: `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/plist/gnu-transcript.txt`, `divergence-probe.txt`
rows.romacs: VM2 matches GNU for every other key and case in that transcript, on interned and uninterned symbols alike (`crates/romacs-vm/tests/symbol_plists.rs`): identity-owned plists, any `eq` key, replace in place, append at the end, `plistp`/`circular-list`/`symbolp` signals, nil/t/keyword plists, buffer-local tables kept off the plist. It differs in four ways. (a) `error-conditions` and `error-message` live in VM2's condition registry, not on the plist: `symbol-plist` omits them and `setplist` neither installs nor removes them, so a condition defined only through `setplist` is unknown to `signal` (it is still caught by an `error` handler, as undefined conditions are, but reports `peculiar error: 1` instead of `C!: 1`), and `symbol-plist` after `define-error` is nil instead of GNU's `(error-conditions ... error-message ...)`. (b) `overriding-plist-environment` has its native nil default and dynamic binding; bulk text-property authorization consults it, but general `get` still ignores it (the probe answers nil, GNU 9). (c) A command compiled from `(interactive ...)` carries the VM-internal property `#:interactive` on its plist (GNU keeps the spec in the function object), so `symbol-plist` shows it (live: `(#:interactive (""))` for `(defun f () (interactive) 1)`, GNU nil) and `setplist` removes it. (d) Properties GNU's own C and preloaded Lisp put on symbols are absent until the code that puts them runs in VM2: in batch GNU, `(symbol-plist nil)` is `(event-symbol-element-mask (nil 0) event-symbol-elements (nil) modifier-cache ((0)))` (keyboard.c) and `(symbol-plist t)` adds `cl--class` (cl-preloaded.el); VM2 answers nil for both (primh pins `symbol-plist/0000`, `0001`, `0024`, `0025`, VALUE)
rows.why: **Package-observable** for (a) to (c): code that copies or inspects whole plists (`symbol-plist`, `setplist`, `cl-remprop`-style edits) sees the registry properties missing and a stray `#:interactive`; the byte compiler's `overriding-plist-environment` bindings have no effect. Image-published plists are now private at restoration, preserving aliases through `put` (former item (d), retired by `code_image::image_alias_tests`). Before this row VM2 had no `symbol-plist`/`setplist` at all and refused `get`/`put` on uninterned symbols with `(error "symbol required")`

rows.mechanism: Non-eager regime caches a body's expansion at its first call
rows.gnu: Before `internal-macroexpand-for-load` is fbound, `readevalloop` (`src/lread.c:2183-2188`) evaluates through `eval_sub`, which expands each body form **when it is reached, on every reach, with no cache**: a macro redefined after a function's first call is used by the next call, a macro's expander runs once per reach, and an unreached form is never expanded. Oracle `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/lazy-bodies-oracle.txt`: `(f1 t)` twice expands twice; after redefining the macro `(f1 t)` => `[1]`
rows.romacs: VM2 holds the body unexpanded (traced heap data, `crates/romacs-vm/LAZY-BODIES.md`) and expands **the whole body once, at the first call**, then runs the cached compiled code; only forms whose expansion FAILS are deferred to their reach and re-expanded on every reach until one succeeds. So: an expander runs once, at the first call, not at each reach; a macro redefined after the first call is not seen by that function; a successfully expandable form in a branch that is never taken is still expanded at the first call
rows.why: **Package-observable** only through macro side effects or macro redefinition between calls of a function defined before macroexp.el is loaded, i.e. during the bootstrap chain (subr.el and anything else loaded before `emacs-lisp/macroexp`). Files loaded after macroexp.el are in GNU's eager regime, where VM2 already matches GNU's timing. Compiling per form on every reach would mean interpreting

rows.mechanism: The eager regime is VM2's compiler, not `internal-macroexpand-for-load`
rows.gnu: Once `internal-macroexpand-for-load` is fbound, GNU **calls** it on every top-level form (`readevalloop_eager_expand_eval`), so macroexp.el's Lisp expander, its `macroexp--pending-eager-loads` `skip` protocol and cycle detection decide expansion, and a failure is the error `Eager macro-expansion failure: ERR`. `eval` never expands eagerly
rows.romacs: VM2 only tests `fboundp internal-macroexpand-for-load` to choose the regime (once per `load`, like GNU); in the eager regime its own compiler expands the whole form, so the function is never called, `macroexp--pending-eager-loads` is not consulted, and a failure reports VM2's own text (the macro's condition text, or a native-expander message), not `Eager macro-expansion failure: ...`. `eval` follows the regime of the load that is running (eager outside any non-eager load), where GNU's `eval` is always non-eager
rows.why: **Package-observable:** a redefinition of `internal-macroexpand-for-load` does not change expansion; loadup's pcase `'(skip)` dance does not make pcase.el lazy; error text of an eager failure differs; an `eval`'d definition whose body fails to expand fails at the `eval` in eager context where GNU defers it to the call

rows.mechanism: A symbol whose function is a special form
rows.gnu: `eval_sub` (`src/eval.c`) dispatches on the head's function when the form is evaluated: `(defalias 'my-progn (symbol-function 'progn))` makes `(my-progn ...)` the special form, as byte-run.el's `(defalias 'inline 'progn)` makes `inline`
rows.romacs: A call whose head names, through aliases, a special form is compiled as that form, when the form is compiled (`Vm::special_form_alias`); an alias made later, or by the same top-level form that calls it, is called as a function and signals `(invalid-function #<subr progn>)`
rows.why: **Package-observable** only for a special-form alias made after the code that calls it is compiled; bytecomp's `inline` and every alias GNU's Lisp makes before use behave as in GNU (`tests/bytecomp_function_value.rs`)

rows.gnu: `Finterpreted_function_p` (`src/data.c:541`) is t iff the object is a closure whose code slot is a cons: any function from `.el` source (eagerly expanded or not), never a subr or byte-code. In a dumped GNU the preloaded functions are byte-compiled, so `(interpreted-function-p (symbol-function 'add-hook))` => nil there and t only in `bootstrap-emacs`
rows.romacs: VM2 has no byte-code: every closure it builds from Lisp source answers t, every primitive nil (oracle rows: `car` nil, `nil` nil, `(lambda (x) x)` t, arity `(1 . 1)`). It does NOT report whether a body is still unexpanded, and neither does GNU's
rows.why: **Package-observable** for preloaded (subr.el, files.el, ...) functions, which answer t where a dumped GNU answers nil; `loadup.el:181` therefore takes its bootstrap-emacs branch and requires gv. `compiled-function-p`/`byte-code-function-p` are not implemented

rows.gnu: In the non-eager regime GNU signals whatever the reached form signals: an unknown head such as a not-yet-loaded `setf` is `(void-function setf)` (gv.el not loaded) or gv's own error, an invalid lambda list is `(invalid-function ...)` at the call, and the interpreted closure keeps only the variables it captures once cconv is loaded
rows.romacs: A deferred form whose failure came from a Lisp macro re-signals that macro's structured condition (matches GNU, test `reach_time_expansion_keeps_a_non_error_condition_structured`); a failure from VM2's **native** expanders (native `setf` places, malformed special forms) signals `(error "MESSAGE")` with VM2's text. A malformed lambda list is still rejected when the closure is created, not when it is called. A lazily held closure captures every visible lexical binding until its first call
rows.why: **Package-observable:** `condition-case` on a reached native-`setf` failure sees `error`, not `void-function`; a defun with an invalid argument list fails at definition. Capturing the whole environment only retains memory

rows.mechanism: `make-variable-buffer-local` of a void variable leaves its default void
rows.gnu: `Fmake_variable_buffer_local` (`src/data.c:2178`, line 2214) sets a void variable's default value to nil before making it automatically buffer-local, so `(progn (make-variable-buffer-local 'v) (default-boundp 'v))` is t
rows.romacs: VM2's `make-variable-buffer-local` installs the local table without touching the default, so the default stays void: `default-boundp` (which itself matches GNU on every other harness row) answers nil, and `default-value`/reading the variable in a buffer without a local signal `void-variable`. The one pinned `default-boundp` harness row, `default-boundp/0034`, is exactly this
rows.why: **Package-observable** for code that makes a never-set variable automatically buffer-local and then reads its default; a `defvar` with a value first (the usual pattern) behaves as in GNU

rows.mechanism: Only the built-in (C) variables the bootstrap reaches exist, with C-time values
rows.gnu: GNU defines 948 variables in C (618 `DEFVAR_LISP`, 196 `DEFVAR_BOOL`, 74 `DEFVAR_INT`, 60 `DEFVAR_PER_BUFFER`); each symbol is `SYMBOL_FORWARDED` to C storage from startup, and a dumped GNU then runs `loadup.el`'s Lisp, which fills several of them (`minibuffer-local-map` gains its bindings, `window-persistent-parameters` gains `(context . writable)`, `load-file-rep-suffixes` gains `".gz"` from jka-cmpr-hook.el)
rows.romacs: VM2 forwards the subset declared in `crates/romacs-vm/src/forwarded.rs`, with each entry citing its DEFVAR and the census or chain need that pulled it in, with GNU's forwarding semantics for `symbol-value`, `set`/`setq`, `let` (including unwinding on a signal), `default-value`, `set-default`, `makunbound` (`Built-in variable may not be unbound`), bool coercion, int `integerp` checks and per-buffer auto-local behaviour; GNU 32.0.50 transcripts in `crates/romacs-vm/evidence/c-variables/`. Values are the C initial values, not the dumped image's: `minibuffer-local-map` is `(keymap)`, `window-persistent-parameters` is `((clone-of . t))`, `load-file-rep-suffixes` is `("")`, so `(get-load-suffixes)` is `(".so" ".elc" ".el")` where `emacs -Q` gives `(".so" ".elc" ".elc.gz" ".el" ".el.gz")` (pinned rows `get-load-suffixes/0000`, `/0002`). Other GNU built-ins are ordinary symbols: void until Lisp sets them, not special unless `defvar`ed, and any value is accepted
rows.why: **Package-observable:** reading an undefined built-in signals `void-variable`; a `let` of one binds lexically under `lexical-binding`; VM2 does not look for compressed `.el.gz` files. Grows as the census pulls variables in, never speculatively (R216), except that all 60 of buffer.c's `DEFVAR_PER_BUFFER` variables exist, as buffers own them together

rows.gnu: `make-local-variable` / `make-variable-buffer-local` of a `DEFVAR_LISP`/`BOOL`/`INT` variable turns it into `SYMBOL_LOCALIZED` over the forwarding (`src/data.c:2178-2300`, a `blv` whose `fwd` is the C storage), and set-buffer swaps the current buffer's binding into that storage, so C reads it: `(with-temp-buffer (make-local-variable 'undo-limit) (setq undo-limit 5) (list undo-limit (default-value 'undo-limit)))` => `(5 160000)`
rows.romacs: VM2 localizes Boolean, integer and object built-ins through the traced local-binding tables, keeping the default in the native storage: a Boolean binding stores t or nil, an integer binding signals `(wrong-type-argument integerp X)` for a non-integer, as GNU's store does. Evaluation reads the current buffer's binding of `max-lisp-eval-depth` (eshell's `setq-local`). The collector's pacing reads only the defaults of `gc-cons-threshold` and `gc-cons-percentage`; every other reader goes through variable lookup and sees the binding. Localized Boolean defaults and saved defaults accept only nil or t; noncanonical writes, or promotion while a saved default is noncanonical, signal an explicit VM2 error. GNU can retain a raw default (`(set-default 'undo-limit 'z)` in a buffer where it is local) until a buffer transition synchronizes its C storage and signals; VM2 checks it at once. Code images retain the existing refusal of localized state
rows.why: **Package-observable** for a buffer-local GC threshold, raw localized integer defaults and noncanonical localized Boolean defaults. eshell's `max-lisp-eval-depth`, compilation and grep buffers' `overlay-arrow-string`, GNU help's and JSON formatting's Booleans localize as in GNU (`tests/localized_bool.rs`, romacs-vm-gui `tests/buffer_locals.rs`)

rows.mechanism: Invalid representation suffix signals instead of crashing
rows.gnu: GNU 32.0.50 `Fget_load_suffixes` (`src/lread.c:961`) exits 139 (SIGSEGV) for `(progn (setq load-file-rep-suffixes (list 42)) (get-load-suffixes))`; its concatenation does not check the element type
rows.romacs: VM2's checked `concat` signals `(wrong-type-argument sequencep 42)` instead. Regression `get_load_suffixes_rejects_gnu_crashing_rep_suffix` rejects a mutant that silently returns nil
rows.why: **Intentional safety divergence:** malformed input is catchable with `condition-case`, never a process crash

rows.mechanism: Empty strings are not one shared object
rows.gnu: GNU has exactly two empty strings, `empty_unibyte_string` and `empty_multibyte_string` (`src/alloc.c:1557-1562`), and every length-0 string allocation returns one of them (`src/alloc.c:2330,2359`), including `copy-sequence` of `""` and a string emptied by `delete` (`src/fns.c:2137`): `(eq (copy-sequence "") (copy-sequence ""))` is t
rows.romacs: VM2 allocates a fresh empty string each time, so that witness is nil (true before `delete` existed). `delete` itself follows GNU exactly: it returns SEQ when nothing matched and a new string of SEQ's kind otherwise; only the identity of an emptied result differs. The one pinned `delete` harness row, `delete/0680` (`(eq r a0)` for two `(copy-sequence "")`), is exactly this
rows.why: **Package-observable** only through `eq` (or `memq`/`assq`) between separately produced empty strings; `equal`, `string=`, length and multibyteness agree. A canonical empty string belongs in the allocator, not in each primitive

rows.gnu: GNU's C maintains both while it loads: `load` specbinds `current-load-list` to `(FILE)` (`loadhist_initialize`, `src/lread.c:1031-1035`), `build_load_history` (`src/lread.c:2054-2114`) moves it into `load-history`, and `load` then calls `do-after-load-evaluation` (`src/lread.c:1539-1540`); `LOADHIST_ATTACH` (`src/lisp.h:4735-4739`) conses onto `current-load-list` from `defvar` (`src/eval.c:913`), `defalias` (`src/data.c:979`), `defvaralias` (`src/eval.c:721`), `provide` and `require` (`src/fns.c:3759`, `src/fns.c:3824`). Harness rows `defvar/036` and `defvar/038`: after `(defvar current-load-list 99)` GNU's `current-load-list` is a new cons, so `(eq current-load-list old)` is nil
rows.romacs: Romacs binds `current-load-list` to `(FILE)` for each load, with FILE the name the file was found by (expanded, not resolved through symlinks, as GNU's `hist_file_name`), replaces the file's `load-history` entry with it when the load completes, then calls `do-after-load-evaluation`; `provide` funcalls its `after-load-alist` entry (`tests/real_ert_load.rs`). `defalias` attaches `(defun . SYMBOL)` (`tests/load_history_defun.rs`), so `symbol-file` finds a function's file; variable declarations can attach entries, but `autoload`, `defvar`, `provide` and `require` do not. Backtraces therefore lack source-file cross-references from load history. `eval-buffer` and `eval-region` remain unsupported, so `eval-buffer-list` stays nil. The two rows above remain pinned VALUE
rows.why: **Package-observable** for code that inspects `current-load-list` or what `load-history` records about definitions (`symbol-file`, `unload-feature`, `find-function` by load history)

rows.mechanism: Loader failures outside Lisp runtime execution remain textual
rows.gnu: GNU runtime signals escaping `load`, `require` and `autoload-do-load` retain their condition and data
rows.romacs: Lisp runtime loading now carries the original condition, data object and selected handler across loader reentry before cleanup. Live GNU comparisons cover ordinary errors, primitive type errors, cyclic aliases, require and autoload signals; returning-handler tests also retain the same error object through GC and unwind. The Rust embedder `load_file` interface still returns textual errors, and source-read/compile failures without a runtime escape use that interface. Compile-time macro-autoload placement remains VM2-LAZY4
rows.why: **Package-observable** for source-read/compile failures; ordinary runtime signals retain their payload

rows.mechanism: Re-entrant `load` of a file already being loaded
rows.gnu: `Fload` refuses a file only when it is already being loaded more than three times (`src/lread.c:1309-1314`, "Recursive load"); `Frequire` refuses a feature only when it is already being required more than three times (`src/fns.c`, "Recursive `require' for feature `%s'"). `provide` takes effect when evaluated, so a file that provides before requiring its partner (calendar.el:163 then :164) satisfies the partner's `require` mid-load; a file whose partner requires it BEFORE it provides is loaded again, nested, and that is fine in GNU. Measured (`crates/romacs-vm/evidence/autoload-load/cyclic-require.txt`): loading calendar, org, org-agenda, gnus and vc-git from source makes 892 requires with 7 re-entrant ones, 6 already satisfied by an early `provide` and ONE genuine nested reload, `gnus-sum.el` required again from `gnus-group.el`
rows.romacs: `provide` is immediate in VM2 too, so every early-provide cycle (calendar/cal-menu, cl-lib/cl-macs, cl-lib/cl-seq) behaves as in GNU, and the late-provide cycle errors as GNU does (condition `error`, VM2's text). But VM2's loader refuses ANY re-entrant load of a file still being loaded ("recursive source load"), so a file that loads itself, and the gnus-sum/gnus-group shape, fail where GNU succeeds (fixture: GNU `(gs 2 (gg gs))`, VM2 `(error)`)
rows.why: **Package-observable** for Gnus (`gnus-sum`) and any file that re-enters its own load. Org and calendar do not need it. Not changed by vm2/autoload; belongs to the loader

rows.mechanism: A symbol with an empty name prints as nothing
rows.gnu: `print_object`, Lisp_Symbol arm (`src/print.c:2496-2500`): with `print-gensym` nil (or for an interned symbol) a zero-byte name prints `##`, so `(prin1-to-string (intern ""))` and `(prin1-to-string (make-symbol ""))` are both `"##"`
rows.romacs: VM2's printer emits the empty name verbatim, so both are `""` (and `(list (intern "") (make-symbol ""))` prints `( )`); true before `keywordp` existed (the 23deaa2a binary gives the same rows). The symbols themselves agree: `symbol-name`, `eq` and `keywordp` (nil for both, harness rows `keywordp/0026`, `/0027`). The two pinned `keywordp` harness rows, `keywordp/0071` and `/0079`, are the printer family of these two values and call no `keywordp`
rows.why: **Package-observable** only when printing the empty-named symbol (`prin1`, `format "%S"`), whose GNU output `##` reads back as that symbol and VM2's empty output does not. Belongs in the printer, not in any primitive

rows.gnu: GNU's initial obarray is a bucket-ordered table, counts every symbol, resets an invalid current `obarray` to the initial table before signalling, and permits removing its nil/t symbols.
rows.romacs: VM2's initial object lazily projects the existing compiler name table. `mapatoms` uses stable slot order (custom tables use GNU bucket order), its printed count includes only subsequent explicit insertions, nil/t remain canonical, and invalid current bindings are rejected without GNU's reset. Live witnesses `evidence/obarray-substrate/divergence-probes.json`: `invalid-current-reset` is GNU t / VM2 nil; filtered initial order differs. Removing compiler-known names also retains existing name-keyed compiler/variable metadata.
rows.why: **Package-observable default-table limitations**, not full initial-obarray parity. Custom obarray lookup, identity, removal, iteration and GC are independently tested.

rows.gnu: GNU accepts arbitrary Emacs strings, comparing both exact bytes and character count.
rows.romacs: Custom obarrays retain exact input-name objects and compare bytes/characters, but construction still requires a Unicode-decodable name for the existing symbol-slot metadata. `(intern (unibyte-string 255) (obarray-make))` signals `not-unicode-string`; GNU returns a symbol. The initial name table also conflates equal UTF-8 bytes with differing character counts. Live transcript: `evidence/obarray-substrate/divergence-probes.json`, `raw-name`. Existing name-based constant checks described in VM2-BOOT4 can also affect custom symbols.
rows.why: **Package-observable symbol-substrate boundary**; no byte coercion or invented replacement symbol is returned.

rows.mechanism: Reader and image integration of obarrays
rows.gnu: GNU's reader interns into the current `obarray`, and its dumped runtime retains the initial obarray.
rows.romacs: VM2's existing reader still interns source names into the compiler name table: `(let ((obarray (obarray-make))) (eq (car (read-from-string "obarray-gap-x")) (intern "obarray-gap-x" obarray)))` is GNU t / VM2 nil (live transcript in `evidence/obarray-substrate/divergence-probes.json`). First-class obarrays are mutable heap objects, so the existing immutable-string/cons-only code-image publisher refuses them; this slice does not add an image codec or alter bootstrap/loadup. Constructing an evaluated call whose head is a custom symbol also reaches the existing generated-symbol compiler restriction (`generated-call-head` in the same transcript: GNU 1, VM2 `symbol required`); ordinary `(funcall SYMBOL)` does not need that source conversion.
rows.why: **Package-observable integration boundaries** outside the custom-collection API. Completion can consume an explicitly supplied obarray through the leaf cursor without relying on reader redirection.

rows.mechanism: General formatting and initial locale capability
rows.gnu: `format-message` has all `format` conversions and text-property/identity behavior; the initial internal quoting flag follows the process locale.
rows.romacs: Quote selection, template-only substitution, explicit capability bindings, display-table fallback and byte8 promotion are implemented. The shared formatter supports field numbers, flags, width and precision for `%s`, `%S`, `%c`, `%d`, `%i`, `%b`, `%B`, `%o`, `%x`, `%X`, `%e`, `%f`, `%g` and `%%`, including bignum integers and float rounding. Width, precision and field-number components are capped at 2^20. Text properties propagate as in `format` (VM2-FMT1), except on the path that promotes raw octets beside Unicode text, which returns no properties; GNU string-identity behavior remains unsupported. Initial capability is the VM UTF-8 default (`t`), without host non-UTF-8 locale detection, and the capability binding is not boolean-normalized.
rows.why: `tests/format_numeric.rs` compares the formatting domain with pinned GNU; the separate 64-case quoting corpus does not establish text-property, identity or host-locale parity.

rows.gnu: GNU `lread.c:openp` checks the suffixed candidate for a `file-exists-p` handler, then uses `file-readable-p` when selected; expansion can also dispatch `expand-file-name`. `fileio.c:find-file-name-handler` selects the latest-starting matching regexp (first on ties), respects handler `operations` and operation-specific inhibition, ignores case-fold-search, and preserves match data.
rows.romacs: As GNU: a selected `file-exists-p` handler makes `file-readable-p` decide, and a function predicate's non-`dir-ok` verdict asks `file-directory-p`, both through Lisp, so their handlers run.
rows.why: Regression coverage: `tests/locate_file_handlers.rs`; oracle pin `45b0f7699df36b3849edc3bdef37d4cb9e75b9ea`, GNU 32.0.50.

rows.section: Observable by a package: mini-window display
rows.gnu: Redisplay shows every window's overlay `before-string` and `after-string` (xdisp.c load_overlay_strings) and resizes the mini-window to its display within `max-mini-window-height` as `resize-mini-windows` says (resize_mini_window; loadup.el sets `grow-only`).
rows.romacs: The mini-window shows its buffer's overlay strings in load_overlay_strings' order, with their `face` properties (a face list merged as xfaces.c does) and a `cursor` property placing point, and redisplay sizes it as resize_mini_window does, including `redisplay-adhoc-scroll-in-resize-mini-windows`; the shared chain sets `grow-only` after window.el as loadup.el does. Other windows show no overlay strings yet; strings' own `display`, `invisible` and image properties are not interpreted; a tab in a string shows as spaces and other controls as `^X`; lines do not wrap, so a line counts once however wide.
rows.why: Completion UIs (icomplete, fido) display their candidates this way. Other windows' point visibility and scrolling count buffer lines (redisplay.rs), which overlay strings would invalidate, so they stay out until that counts display lines. `crates/romacs-vm/tests/mini_window.rs`; the GUI journey `crates/romacs-vm-gui/tests/gnu_completion.rs` and `harness/completion_live.py`.

rows.section: Observable by a package: circular completion tables
rows.gnu: GNU traverses until an exact test match, a decisive common prefix, or user quit; some circular inputs never finish.
rows.romacs: Decisive early results are preserved. Traversal that would revisit a detected cycle signals `circular-list`.
rows.why: Bounded native traversal with callback state traced across GC. `tests/completion.rs` covers both early-result cases.

rows.section: Observable by a package: circular completion tables
rows.mechanism: Completion case folding, string comparison and casing
rows.gnu: GNU uses its current case tables, with nil entries meaning identity.
rows.romacs: Original native tables retain Unicode fallback for nil entries above ASCII before GNU enrichment. Explicit non-nil entries override it; ASCII and replacement-table nil entries mean identity.
rows.why: Preserve the native Unicode startup policy while respecting explicit ASCII edits and replacement tables. Range-crossing and replacement-table tests cover the boundary.

rows.mechanism: Closure metadata and GNU generic dispatch
rows.gnu: GNU OClosure inspects closure documentation and captured environment slots.
rows.romacs: Ordinary closures retain a private traced documentation value. The explicit `oclosure--fix-type` marker emitted by GNU's macro retains named capture cells and exposes the supported interpreter metadata. `romacs-cl-generic` loads the owned `romacs-oclosure` type-query bridge before unchanged GNU `cl-generic`.
rows.why: Compatibility callers must load the named entry after GNU core prerequisites; this is not an automatic GUI startup addition. Ordinary closure array access remains rejected. Explicit OClosure capture retention may include bindings GNU optimizes away. Existing code-image restrictions on mutable captured cells remain. Code images use VM2CODE8 to serialize private documentation. `tests/oclosure.rs` covers accessors, copying, inheritance, identity, GC, dispatch, replacement and method combination.

rows.mechanism: Explicit batch adapter and compiled backtrace metadata
rows.gnu: ERT isolates each test with a temporary buffer and a window excursion; GNU backtraces can describe interpreter/source frames and lexical locals.
rows.romacs: The named `romacs-batch` adapter retains the temporary buffer, assertions, error handling, cleanup, expectedness and GNU batch runner, and replaces the precautionary window excursion. Condition objects use `prin1` plus a newline instead of editor indentation; their data and expectedness are unchanged. Automatic window-layout restoration and GUI fixtures are unsupported. Backtraces report real compiled calls, original evaluated argument snapshots and dynamic locals; lexical/source locals, pre-argument named-autoload frames and debugger mutation are unavailable. GNU apply optimizations can produce different frame/argument shapes. Ordinary closures print opaquely through an owned `cl-print-object` method.
rows.why: Keep the batch regime explicit and preserve private closure representation.

rows.mechanism: Bulk text-property edits and forward boundary queries
rows.gnu: GNU supports arbitrary property keys, modification callbacks, byte buffers and raw interval traversal with `next-property-change` LIMIT t.
rows.romacs: Bulk edits support interned symbol keys, mutable strings and annotated text buffers, with atomic validation, read-only checks and a changed-result flag. Unibyte buffers are edited too, and change hooks run as VM2-EDIT-HOOKS1 describes. Other key types and immutable image-string writes refuse explicitly. The two forward queries support strings and annotated text buffers; unibyte-buffer queries and raw interval LIMIT t refuse explicitly. Effective property queries retain the existing general property-resolution limits.
rows.why: Reuse the native property runs and overlay precedence for the ERT printer's actual calls.

rows.section: Observable by a user: workspace file coding
rows.mechanism: File coding in the default workspace (no loadup)
rows.gnu: GNU's image has all of mule-conf.el and the language environments; `set-locale-environment` for a UTF-8 locale on GNU/Linux puts `utf-8` first in `coding-system-priority-list` and makes the default `buffer-file-coding-system` and `default-file-name-coding-system` `utf-8-unix`. Visiting also consults `set-auto-coding-function` (`set-auto-coding`: `auto-coding-alist`, `auto-coding-regexp-alist`, `coding:` cookies, `auto-coding-functions`) and `file-coding-system-alist`; saving consults `select-safe-coding-system-function` (`select-safe-coding-system`, which asks through `select-safe-coding-system-interactively` when no default coding system encodes the text, and warns and asks before writing under a cookie that names an unknown coding system), and `basic-save-buffer-2` keeps `last-coding-system-used` as `buffer-file-coding-system`.
rows.romacs: Startup (`initialize_coding`, `crates/romacs-vm-gui/src/startup.rs`) evaluates verbatim from the pinned mirror mule.el's `define-coding-system`, `coding-system-type`, `buffer-file-coding-system-explicit`, `after-insert-file-set-coding` and `find-new-buffer-file-coding-system`, and mule-conf.el's fundamental aliases, `prefer-utf-8`, `raw-text`, `no-conversion-multibyte`, `iso-latin-1` (`iso-8859-1`, `latin-1`), the `utf-8`, `utf-8-with-signature`, `utf-8-auto` and `utf-8-emacs` definitions with their aliases, and the `latin-extra-code-table` entries. It also evaluates mule.el's auto-coding machinery (`auto-coding-alist`, `auto-coding-regexp-alist`, `auto-coding-functions` with `sgml-xml-auto-coding-function` and `sgml-html-meta-auto-coding-function`, `find-auto-coding`, `set-auto-coding`, `coding-system-get`, `coding-system-category`, `coding-system-equal`) and its `(setq set-auto-coding-function ...)`, and mule-cmds.el's `select-safe-coding-system` with `find-coding-systems-region`, `sort-coding-systems`, `coding-system-change-eol-conversion`, `coding-system-change-text-conversion`, `get-language-info` (`language-info-alist` nil, `current-language-environment` "English") and its `(setq select-safe-coding-system-function ...)`, together with the helpers they call from files.el (`set-auto-mode-1`, `inhibit-local-variables-p`, `file-name-sans-versions`, `find-file-literally`), subr.el (`caar`, `ignore-errors`, `string-match-p`, `ensure-list`), byte-run.el (`defsubst` and its `eval-and-compile`, `function-put`, `byte-run--set-speed`) and mule-util.el (`with-coding-priority`). `rlisp/romacs-coding.el` then sets GNU's UTF-8-locale result restricted to those systems: priority `utf-8 iso-latin-1 raw-text utf-8-auto utf-8-with-signature undecided` and the `utf-8-unix` defaults; it assumes a UTF-8 locale. Its one adaptation replaces the question: the workspace cannot show GNU's *Warning* explanation (temp-buffer display, help buttons, fill), so `select-safe-coding-system-interactively` signals `romacs-unsafe-coding` with the unsafe defaults and the safe systems GNU would offer; `write-region` has not opened the file, which keeps its bytes, and the buffer stays modified. The workspace save (`romacs-gui-write-visited-buffer`, `rlisp/romacs-startup.el`) keeps `last-coding-system-used` as GNU's `basic-save-buffer-1` and `-2` do. No other coding system is defined (ISO-2022, UTF-16, CJK, other ISO-8859 sets), and `file-coding-system-alist` stays nil.
rows.why: UTF-8 (LF and CRLF), ASCII and Latin-1 files (with or without a cookie, agreeing with the bytes or not) and a UTF-8 file with a BOM visit, edit and save as pinned GNU does: decoded text, `last-coding-system-used`, `buffer-file-coding-system` and bytes on disk, including λ typed into a Latin-1 file (saved as UTF-8) and text typed before a BOM (kept after the signature) (`crates/romacs-vm-gui/src/command.rs` `coding_journey_visits_edits_and_saves_as_pinned_gnu`); where pinned GNU asks (λ under a `coding: latin-1` cookie) C-x C-s signals `romacs-unsafe-coding` with GNU's unsafe defaults and its safe systems that the workspace defines, before writing (`coding_save_refuses_where_pinned_gnu_would_ask`). **User-observable**: (1) where GNU asks which coding system to save with, the workspace refuses the save; (2) a cookie or signature naming a coding system the workspace does not define (e.g. `coding: euc-jp`, a UTF-16 BOM) is ignored by the visit, which detection decides, and saving then signals `void-function display-warning` before writing where GNU warns and asks `Really proceed with writing?` (warnings.el is absent); (3) `detect-coding-region` is not implemented, so GNU's `sgml-xml-auto-coding-function` fails inside its `ignore-errors` for an XML declaration without `encoding=`, and detection decides (`undecided-unix` for ASCII XML where GNU names `utf-8-unix`); (4) bytes only an undefined coding detects (C1 bytes outside `latin-extra-code-table`, which GNU decodes as `japanese-shift-jis`; UTF-16; ISO-2022) refuse the visit (`raw bytes into a multibyte buffer` or a detector refusal), leaving the file untouched.

rows.mechanism: `emacs-build-time` in a VM restored from a world
rows.gnu: A dumped GNU reports the time its dump was made: `version.el:79-84` runs in loadup, and pdumper restores its value without evaluating it again.
rows.romacs: A VM booted from source reports its own clock at `version.el`; one restored from a world reports the time the world was built, as a dumped GNU does.
rows.why: **Package-observable** only through that one value: every other value a restored VM holds is a function of the binary, the recipe and its keyed host facts, or is rebuilt (`romacs-world-restart`). gnu-tests/tools/world-diff-allow.txt lists it.

rows.mechanism: Where a process booted from a world keeps its heap
rows.gnu: GNU restores its dump at any address: pdumper relocates every pointer.
rows.romacs: A world image is the heap of the process that built it, mapped back at its own addresses (`world::arena`): the arena's address is random per world, not per process. Everything else a world process maps keeps address randomization, the executable too. The image addresses only read-only data of the builder's executable (literals, constant tables, vtables); a restored process maps a read-only copy of those segments where the builder had them and leaves the rest of that range inaccessible, so an image holds no code address that could be followed.
rows.why: Not package-observable. Someone who can read the world store learns where a world process keeps its heap; `ROMACS_WORLD=off` boots from source, with a heap at a per-process random address. The store defends against accidental change, not against a writer with the user's own permissions: a world is refused and rebuilt after a truncated or partly written image, an interrupted build, an upgraded binary or library (keyed by content and by each library's build-id and mapped constant bytes), and corruption that changes a file's identity or times. It deliberately does not detect a same-user writer, who can already edit the user's init file, the store's images and the binaries themselves (one can, say, record an old digest under a damaged image's metadata); bit rot that leaves size and times unchanged, since the image and executable digests are cached by file identity; or writes to a mapped image or library after it was checked.

rows.mechanism: The libraries a user's init loads, in a VM restored from a world
rows.gnu: GNU dumps only its own preloaded Lisp; every library the init requires loads from source or bytecode in each session, and its load-time `defcustom`, `defvar` and `defconst` forms evaluate in that process (`executable-find`, `locate-user-emacs-file`, `(getenv ...)`).
rows.romacs: A live `--loadup` launch that loads the init restores the init's layer when the store holds one (`romacs_vm::world::layer`, `crates/romacs-vm-gui/src/world.rs`): the base world plus the libraries the init's recorded plan loads, replayed after the chain under each entry's recorded `load-path`. The plan is the `require` and autoload calls the init itself issued, recorded while it ran; a launch without a current layer boots from the base world, records the plan again and builds the layer ahead of the next launch. A layer's definition form that reads a per-process fact is kept and evaluated again at restore (`romacs--world-reseed-forms`: a `defcustom` through `custom-reevaluate-setting`, the others by their value form), as GNU's delayed init re-evaluates its dumped options; a definition a refused effect cuts short (a `make-directory`) is deferred whole. Any other form's such read, an effect, a signal or a timer left behind refuses its entry, which then loads from source as before. The startup function runs again in the builder after the libraries, as a restored process runs it after them, and must compute what it computed before them.
rows.why: **Package-observable** in four ways. A library's load-time code sees the standard value of a variable the init sets before requiring it, since the layer loaded the library first (the init's own `setq` still applies after). A hook function a library adds when it loads precedes, in `add-hook`'s order, the ones the init adds, where a source session has the init's first (`kill-emacs-hook`: the init's savers run before org-persist's). A library's load-time code runs with the chain's initial terminal, not the session's display: `window-system` and `display-graphic-p` answer nil there, where a source session's library finds the pgtk frame (`noninteractive` is nil in both). A `require` the init issues only under a condition that differs between sessions is replayed from the previous session's plan: the layer may hold a library this session's init would not have loaded; the next launch plans afresh. A library edit, a package update, a changed `load-path`, an edited init, another build or another base world rebuilds or bypasses the layer: every file a layer build read is a keyed record of its manifest, the plan's digest and the base world's key are in the layer's key, and the init's content digest is checked at the launch. `ROMACS_WORLD=off` boots from source.
